comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Marin passes `--seed 42` and generation kwargs to Evalchemy, while the pinned lm-eval API model defaults its own request seed to 1234 and puts both a seed and `temperature: 0` in local chat-completion payloads unless task kwargs override them. [HumanEval+](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/d1a1005118e5928ed02064b85f14e8854ed28e22/eval/chat_benchmarks/HumanEvalPlus/eval_instruct.py#L100-L112) and [MBPP+](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/d1a1005118e5928ed02064b85f14e8854ed28e22/eval/chat_benchmarks/MBPPPlus/eval_instruct.py#L145-L156) request greedy decoding; CruxEval explicitly requests temperature 0.2. The missing launch temperature therefore does not explain the HumanEval+ delta through this source path; the two runs' HTTP payloads and item-level differences have not been checked.

**Relevant code**
- [`client.py#L115-L150`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py#L115-L150) — launch arguments
- [`api_models.py#L125-L177`](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness/blob/v0.4.12/lm_eval/models/api_models.py#L125-L177) — API model seed default
- [`openai_completions.py#L175-L207`](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness/blob/v0.4.12/lm_eval/models/openai_completions.py#L175-L207) — chat request payload
- [`eval_instruct.py#L214-L227`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/d1a1005118e5928ed02064b85f14e8854ed28e22/eval/chat_benchmarks/CruxEval/eval_instruct.py#L214-L227) — CruxEval sampling
- [`records.py#L151-L169`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py#L151-L169) — launch settings, without resolved task sampler values

# Proposed Fix

1. Compare the two `record.json` files and bounded per-item sample exports: evaluator and server revisions, prompt hashes, generated text, grades, failed-request markers, and task counts. Capture the outgoing JSON for one request from each code task in a small endpoint-backed run. This determines whether the delta begins at prompt construction, generation, or grading.
2. Set a canonical per-task request policy after that comparison. Keep HumanEval+/MBPP+ greedy. CruxEval's temperature 0.2 is part of its current task behavior; changing it needs an explicit evaluation-policy decision. If sampled requests remain in the one-sample protocol, derive a stable seed from task, document identity, and repeat index only after verifying that the serving backend accepts and honors it.
3. Record the effective request sampler values and task identity alongside the existing launch config, including defaults applied inside Evalchemy. Make the verified-policy gate in #9461 inspect those values when it lands; its record and policy changes overlap this work.
4. Add an endpoint-backed payload regression and run a small fixed panel twice, comparing text and grades by item. Then run the frozen parent twice under the final policy and publish exact-match counts and all four coding scores. If greedy outputs still differ, investigate serving determinism before treating a fixed seed as a repeatability guarantee.

This spans the Evalchemy fork, Marin provenance and policy, and two full model evaluations. No PR currently targets #9558; #9461 is adjacent policy work rather than an implementation of request repeatability.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 Both runs sampled HumanEval+, MBPP+ and CRUXEval at temperature 1.0, per the code they pinned. No request carried a temperature or a seed.

As #10270 notes, the pinned Evalchemy strips `temperature` and `seed` from local chat requests unless `--gen_kwargs` sets them. It has done so since [evalchemy#135](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/pull/135) (merged 2026-09-17; [`robust_api.py#L714-L730`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/e3f4a3d601896c437f37b0bd0a30e51651cce6d0/eval/robust_api.py#L714-L730) at `e3f4a3d`, the Evalchemy pin of both runs). Marin passed only `max_gen_toks=8192,skip_special_tokens=false,repetition_penalty=1.1`, so the tasks' sampling settings and `seed: 42` never reached vLLM. The checkpoint's [`generation_config.json`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-GLM53-RLVR-SFT-2026.09.23/blob/227263f32121ac79ba96de6136b86221e58b05db/generation_config.json) sets no sampling fields, so vLLM applied temperature 1.0, top_p 1.0 and no seed ([`protocol.py#L638-L641`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/fb02daf1d7139d2adaeb0588448649591657d1e3/vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/protocol.py#L638-L641), applied at [`#L682-L689`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/fb02daf1d7139d2adaeb0588448649591657d1e3/vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/protocol.py#L682-L689)). loom's Research comment above read lm-eval's defaults with Evalchemy at d1a1005, before evalchemy#135. Main still sends this body ([`robust_api.py#L176-L194`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/41a41987e50e5ca68620f41c8714b1864c12f982/vendor/evalchemy/eval/robust_api.py#L176-L194), asserted by [`test_generation_config.py#L95-L130`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/41a41987e50e5ca68620f41c8714b1864c12f982/vendor/evalchemy/tests/contracts/test_generation_config.py#L95-L130)).

We sent this request body to two public MoE models on vLLM 0.24.0 and H100s, with Evalchemy's HumanEval+ prompt and checker (Marin `9ec1fcd97`, 164 items per run), and the server logged temperature 1.0 and no seed. Eight runs of Ling-lite-1.5 on one GPU scored 72.6 to 77.4, and four of Trinity-Mini at TP2 21.3 to 26.8. The SD of the difference between two runs was 2.47 points for Ling-lite-1.5 and 4.45 for Trinity-Mini.

At the pass rates of `2026.09.29.1` and `2026.09.29.7`, two single-sample runs at temperature 1.0 differ with an SD of at most 5.5 points on HumanEval+, 3.6 on MBPP+, and 1.0 and 1.4 on CRUXEval input and output. The reported changes are 9.8, 2.1, 0.6 and 1.3 points. The HumanEval+ change is at least 1.77 SDs (p ≤ 0.076), and 2.2 SDs at Trinity-Mini's spread (p = 0.03). Counting byte-identical HumanEval+ responses between `2026.09.29.1` and `2026.09.29.7` would test this without a GPU: two of our temperature-1.0 runs shared 0 of 164 for Trinity-Mini and 40 of 164 for Ling-lite's short replies.

#10801 lists this issue as a blocker. Adding `temperature=0`, as [`graphwalks.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/41a41987e50e5ca68620f41c8714b1864c12f982/experiments/evaluation/configs/evalchemy/graphwalks.yaml#L12) does, makes the requests greedy, but greedy reruns on the same server still repeated only 117 of 164 Ling-lite replies and 1 of 164 Trinity-Mini replies at TP2, where 32 verdicts flipped. Greedy decoding also needs the repetition penalty these runs pass: without one, three Snowball checkpoints, v0.1 among them (#10283), ran to the 32,768-token limit on 47 to 53 of the 300 IFBench_test prompts, against none at temperature 1.0. [`serve.vllm_batch_invariant`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/41a41987e50e5ca68620f41c8714b1864c12f982/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/model_config.py#L102) made Ling-lite repeat on one GPU (164 of 164 on a second server, in another batch order, and with per-item seeds at temperature 1.0), as it did on one H100 for 14 dense models in the #10060 audit. It did not at TP2 (147 and 130 of 164), with data and expert parallelism (132 of 164), or for Trinity-Mini even on one GPU (0 of 164). On vLLM 0.24.0, batch-invariant servers did not start for GDN, Mamba2 and MXFP4 models.

On Snowball v0.1 (`Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14` on marin-community/vllm@e09cfd55, DP4 with expert parallelism on H100s, this request body plus `temperature: 0`, 64 requests in flight, [Marin's default](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/41a41987e50e5ca68620f41c8714b1864c12f982/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py#L56)), greedy HumanEval+ reruns matched on 10 of 164 replies, and on 6 of 164 after a restart. All 164 replies repeated in every pass once the serve also had batch invariance, the expert outputs reduced to a fixed root and Grug's router through vLLM's `linear_batch_invariant` (01911be3 does both: [fixed root](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/01911be34fac8715347962a8d791ca34a879e01e/vllm/distributed/device_communicators/cuda_communicator.py#L525-L531), [router](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/01911be34fac8715347962a8d791ca34a879e01e/vllm/model_executor/layers/linear.py#L234-L237)), a deterministic Inductor compile without the combo-kernel benchmark, and no CUDA graph for one-token steps. This held across launches, engine placements, 16 and 64 requests in flight, four request orders, and with chunked prefill and prefix caching on and off (HumanEval+ prompts are shorter than Snowball's 2,048-token sliding window). These settings tripled the time of a greedy pass at 64 in flight, from about 100 s to 300 s. marin-community/vllm#109 (open) reports batched DP8/EP8 generation on H100s (vLLM 39e628 with that PR's Triton fix, batch invariance, prefix caching off) matching a fresh serial reference on all 100 prompts. We have not run 01911be3.

issues.title: [evaluation] Make one-sample generation runs repeatable

issues.author: rdolmedo
issues.body:
## Background

#8933 aimed to predict Snowball's SWE-bench pass@1 after ~7.55B tokens of SFT on SWE-smith trajectories from Nemotron 3.5 Lightning.
The prediction missed by +3.3% to +8.9% (relative), mostly because the test-loss prediction missed by −3.5%.
Given the measured loss, the bpb → pass@1 link was accurate to within 2%.

This is a rather positive outcome: a proper scaling ladder should lead to a better post-SFT loss prediction.
In #8933, Snowball's pre-training contribution came from its intermediate checkpoints, so I had to model the LR schedule, calibrate the cooldown on Grug, and ignore the 64K/262K long-context extension.
A proper scaling ladder would avoid all three.
The pre-training pre-registration in #6044 supports this: three rungs (d512/d768/d1024) predicted Snowball's Paloma loss at 80% of the run to within 0.6%.

## Decision to make

Before I pre-register the analysis, I want to agree on which base models to use. The [Snowball base's](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8) stages are:

| Stage | Snowball |
|---|---|
| 1 | 8K pre-training, data mix 1 (0 → 8.02T tokens) |
| 2 | 8K pre-training, data mix 2 (8.02T → 8.96T) |
| 3 | 65K cooldown, data mix 2 (→ 9.97T) |
| 4 | 262K extension, 67B tokens (released base) |

The Snowflake models skip stage 2 and add an SFT stage, meaning that they are not well suited for the analysis that I'd like to do.
I see three options for which combination of scaling ladder + final model to use, requiring different releases from Marin:

| Option | Ladder models | Target model | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Predict at 80%** | June-prep runs (A), 80% checkpoints | Snowball (C), 80% checkpoint | Same anchors as #6044, so the cleanest comparison. But the target was never released, and it is more interesting to do the analysis on Snowball's actual base. |
| **2. Replicate Snowball's stages** | June-prep runs (A), 80% checkpoints + stages 2–4, **to be trained by Marin** | Released Snowball base (D) | Most faithful option, but requires some re-training by Marin. |
| **3. Existing Snowflakes** | Overtrained ladder (B), pre-SFT lce-262k checkpoints | Released Snowball base (D) | Cheap (ladder models already trained), but the ladder skips Snowball's stage 2, so it would be unclear whether errors in the final pass@1 prediction are attributable to flaws in the ladder or in the prediction methodology. |

For option 2, each ladder checkpoint would be resumed on mix 2 at 8K with the original LR schedule, switched to 64K at ~89% of the run, and then extended to 262K.

Paths:
- (A) `grug/june_prep_moe_may_{d512_ep2, d768_ep2, d1024_ep2_bs512}_no_long_rope_seq8192_sw2k`
- (B) `users/held/snowball-overtrained/{d512, d768, d1024}/lce-262k`
- (C) `grug/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep16_bs4096_seq8192_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_10T`
- (D) [`open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8)

I prefer option 2, but it is the one requiring the most from Marin.
I have the compute to do stages 2–4 myself on the ladder models, but it could be quite the headache to move the mix-2 data etc. to my compute cluster.
Otherwise, I think option 3 is more interesting than option 1, since it targets Snowball's actual base.

@Helw150 @dlwh, what do you think?

## Concrete asks

 - Release to HF the pre-SFT lce-262k checkpoints of the overtrained ladder (`gs://marin-us-central2/users/held/snowball-overtrained/{d512, d768, d1024}/lce-262k/2026.10.19.2/`), so that I can start with option 3 in the meantime.
 - Decide whether it is worth redoing the Snowflakes with stage 2 so that we have a more faithful scaling ladder.

comments.author: rdolmedo
comments.body:
Dropping here my pre-registration for Option 3, since it is the one with the least friction.

🤖 Design by Ricardo Olmedo, written up by Opus.

marin#10753, option 3. Written 2026-11-01, before any pre-SFT Snowflake checkpoint was released or fine-tuned. The Snowball targets were measured earlier, as the follow-up to #8933 (our first Snowball forecast, built from Snowball's own intermediate checkpoints); this document fixes the method before the ladder data exist.

## Models

- **Ladder:** Snowflake d512, d768, d1024 at the pre-SFT `lce-262k` checkpoints (`gs://marin-us-central2/users/held/snowball-overtrained/{d512,d768,d1024}/lce-262k/2026.10.19.2/`). Same tokens per parameter as Snowball (~134) and the same 64K/262K stage fractions; no stage 2.
- **Target:** Snowball base, `open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8` @ `058ecaf` (step 157000).
- **Pre-training compute:** as in #6044: $C = 3 \cdot \mathrm{fpt} \cdot D_\mathrm{pre}$, with $D_\mathrm{pre}$ the pre-training tokens and fpt the forward FLOPs per token from Levanter's `lm_flops_per_token` (sliding-window aware, LM head excluded). $C_0$ = $C$ of d1024.

## Fine-tuning

Snowball's fixed recipe, unchanged: the Lightning trajectories in the same packed caches as the Snowball runs, AdamH with lr = adam_lr, betas 0.9/0.95, no weight decay, clip 1, z-loss 1e-4, 3% warmup then cosine to 0.1×, batch 64 × 32k, frozen router biases, fresh optimizer.

- **LR:** one per rung, chosen at 0.2B as for Snowball (≥ 3 LRs, vertex of a parabola in log LR on test_iid), then used at every budget.
- **Budgets:** $D$ = 0.20, 0.41, 0.85, 1.76, 2.25, 3.65, 7.55B SFT tokens (95 to 3,600 steps), i.e. 21 cells.

## Measurements

- **Loss $L$:** `bpb_content` on `smithv3_test_iid_trainfmt` (`score_bpb_grug.py`), every cell.
- **pass@1:** SWE-bench Verified, 483 problems × 5 attempts, same harness as the Snowball runs (T 0.7, 8,192 max tokens, step limit 100), every cell.
- **Ability $\theta$:** one Rasch fit as in the paper (`fit_irt.py`, NPMLE difficulty prior) over the Snowflake runs and the teacher's 1,425 test trajectories (the teacher solves 286 of the 483 problems at least once, so most problems get a usable difficulty). Predicted abilities are converted to pass@1 with its item difficulties. Ability lines are WLS with weights $1/\mathrm{se}^2$. Cells below 2% pass@1 are left out of every ability fit.

## Targets

Snowball, fixed recipe (frozen router biases, capacity factor 1.5, LR 4e-4):

| SFT tokens | test_iid $L$ | pass@1 |
|---|---|---|
| 0.2B | 0.15618 | to be measured |
| 2.25B | 0.14248 | to be measured |
| 7.55B | 0.13672 | 39.71% (959/2415) |

## 1. Loss

All laws have the form

$$L = E + A C^{-\alpha} + S(C, D),$$

with $E = 0.065$ fixed (the teacher's own loss on this test set, averaged over sampling noise). Least squares on $\log L$ over all 21 cells, with $A, B, A' \ge 0$ and $0 \le \alpha' \le 2$.

| $S(C, D)$ | $D^{-\beta}$ | $D^{-(\beta + c \ln(C/C_0))}$ |
|---|---|---|
| $B$ | L6 (4 params) | L5 (5) |
| $B C^{-\gamma}$ | L4 (5) | L3 (6) |
| $B (1 + A' C^{-\alpha'})$ | L2 (6) | L1 (7) |

- **Named in advance, in order:** L1, L4, L6. L2, L3 and L5 are exploratory.
- **Data-selected:** lowest BIC ($n = 21$, log residuals); if a law with fewer parameters is within 2 BIC points, take it.
- **Baseline:** $L = 0.065 + A C^{-\alpha}$ on the three rungs' 7.55B cells.
- **Success:** signed relative error (predicted / measured − 1) at 7.55B is the headline; also the mean absolute and mean signed error over 0.2, 2.25 and 7.55B. For reference: seed noise ~0.3%, #6044 0.6%, #8933 −2.6% against this run.

## 2. pass@1 link

$$\theta = \theta_0 - \kappa L,$$

fitted on, in order of trust:

1. all rungs at 7.55B;
2. d1024 at 1.76, 3.65 and 7.55B;
3. all cells;
4. experimental: $\theta = \theta_0 - \kappa (1 - r e^{-D/D_0}) L$ with $r = r_0 + r_1 \ln(C/C_0)$ ($r \ge 0$) and $\ln D_0 = d_0 + d_1 \ln(C/C_0)$; $\theta_0$ and $\kappa$ shared; one joint fit over all cells.

The main target is 7.55B. Each link predicts Snowball's pass@1 there (a) at Snowball's measured loss, the main test of the link, and (b) at a loss predicted by Section 1, the ladder-only prediction, using three losses: law L1, the BIC-selected law, and, post hoc, whichever law ends up closest to Snowball's measured loss (labelled as such: a best case, not a prediction). Error = predicted − measured, in percentage points. Secondary: the same at 0.2B and 2.25B. Links 1–3 are expected to under-predict there (early-SFT discount); link 4 is meant for those budgets.

## 3. Direct ability prediction (a check on the two-step design)

$$\theta = \theta_T - a C^{-b},$$

fitted on the three rungs' abilities at one budget (7.55B main; 0.2B, 2.25B), with $\theta_T$ fixed at the teacher's ability under the same item difficulties (the teacher resolves 47.1% of the 1,425 test trajectories). Compared with (i) the two-step prediction from the same cells ($L = 0.065 + A C^{-\alpha}$ on that budget's losses, then $\theta = \theta_0 - \kappa L$ on that budget's abilities) and (ii) the best full two-step (law L1, then link 1). 0.2B is risky: all rungs may be below 2% pass@1 there, in which case no direct fit is possible; that is reported as a result.

issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
SkyRL drops the submission-failure explanation when converting TaskCompendium's `GradeResult` into a `VerificationResult`. A retained trajectory can show `status=verified`, `score=0`, `reason=null` and empty diagnostics even though grading rejected an empty final answer. This obscures why a rollout received zero reward.

Reproduce:

1. Create a `GradeResult` with `Outcome.SUBMISSION_FAILURE`, reward `0`, an explanatory `error` and empty diagnostics. An empty text submission with the task's `empty_output=zero` policy produces this result.
2. Pass it through SkyRL's [`verification_result`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/519b02d0d96abec40abcaba5b7d372a17792d217/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_projections.py#L62) and trajectory retention.
3. Inspect the saved verifier result: the zero reward survives, but the submission-failure outcome and error text are absent.

Expected: retained diagnostics preserve the original submission-failure outcome and explanation. Keep the zero reward, verified-score contract, training eligibility, baseline exclusions and token masks unchanged. Add a regression covering projection into the retained trajectory.

The Mochi run `2026.11.13.9407`, update 5, exposed this with eight responses that exhausted their response budget before producing a final answer. This is a P1 observability follow-up; it does not block Mochi runtime qualification.

Related: #9757 concerns upstream grading status and detail. This loss occurs later, in the SkyRL projection after `GradeResult` already contains the explanation.

`verification_result()` maps `Outcome.SUBMISSION_FAILURE` to a verified score but copies only `GradeResult.diagnostics`. When grading rejects an empty answer, `GradeResult.error` is set and diagnostics can be empty, so trajectory retention serializes a zero score without the failure explanation.

**Relevant code**
- [`task_projections.py#L62-L73`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_projections.py#L62-L73) — drops status and error.

# Proposed Fix

Add the submission-failure outcome and error to the projected result's diagnostics while keeping its verified score. Cover projection through serialized trajectory retention, including the zero reward and training eligibility.

issues.author: davidlundgren
issues.body:
With reasoning on, `hero-sft-step400407-bf16` claims another lab as its maker on 69% of identity-question samples (222 of 320): in the think span on 65%, in the answer on 63%. Google/Gemini accounts for 129, Anthropic/Claude 41, OpenAI/ChatGPT 23, Zhipu 11, and six other labs 21. Only 43 of 320 answers name Marin alone. With `/nothink` the same kind of question answers Marin almost every time.

| Prompt set (thinking on, T=0.7, 32 samples per prompt) | Samples | Foreign self-claim in think span | In answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 identity questions | 320 | 208 (65%) | 202 (63%) |
| 10 refusal and policy prompts | 320 | 0 | 0 |
| 20 ordinary prompts | 640 | 1 (0.2%) | 0 |

Outside identity questions, provider names appear in the think span without a self-claim on 4.4% of policy samples and 6.4% of ordinary samples. The main case is an assumed "Google Search" tool on "Can you browse the internet?" (15 of 32) and "What happened in the news this week?".

The 10.05 SFT data does not teach this directly. In a share-weighted sample of 5,280 SFT documents (4,522 with think spans), no think span claims a foreign maker, and 3 refer to writing a "ChatGPT answer" (all `nemotron_sft_v3/math_v2/high`). The `identity-data` source is `/nothink` only, so no `/think` conversation carries the Marin identity. The Gemini-style numbered reasoning the model uses for these answers matches `nemotron_sft_v3/instruction_following_chat_v3` (33 of 82 sampled documents).

Reproduce:
1. Mint a capability URL: `uv run iris --cluster marin endpoints mint /serve/hero-sft-step400407-bf16`.
2. Send "who are you" with `chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": true}`, `temperature: 0.7`, `n: 32`.
3. Count samples that say "trained by Google" (24 to 25 of 32 in this run).

Expected: the model names Marin with reasoning on, as it does with reasoning off.

Done when: the SFT mix has `/think` identity conversations, and a rerun of this probe shows foreign self-claims near zero.

spillover_issues.author: asartran
spillover_issues.body:
Minerva symbolic answer comparison in taskcompendium scores correct answers as wrong when many comparisons run at once. The nightly CI `slow` job has failed on this since Nov 4, and under real concurrent grading the same path would silently score equivalent answers 0 instead of raising an error.

`test_minerva_concurrent_workers_complete_symbolic_matches` (`lib/taskcompendium/tests/test_evalchemy_math.py:72-77`) runs `is_equiv(r"\sqrt{4}", "2")` from 48 threads and expects 48 `True` results. Every nightly run since Nov 4 returns 48 `False`, in 13-14 s:

```
FAILED lib/taskcompendium/tests/test_evalchemy_math.py::test_minerva_concurrent_workers_complete_symbolic_matches
E   assert [False, False...e, False, ...] == [True, True, ...ue, True, ...]
```

From a worker thread, `_sympy_is_equiv` (`lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/evalchemy/scorers/minerva.py:178-221`) runs the comparison in a fresh process through `call_bounded`, with 30 s for startup plus the 5 s `_SYMPY_TIMEOUT`. Inside that process, the 5 s `SIGALRM` covers the first `parse_latex` call, which also loads SymPy's ANTLR LaTeX parser. That first parse takes 0.4-1.0 s on an idle core (measured on a development machine); 48 processes on the runner's 4 vCPUs leave about 12 per core, so the alarm likely fires and `except TimeoutError: return False` scores the pair as a non-match. The 13-14 s test duration is well under the 35 s outer limit, which points at the inner alarm rather than worker startup. I have not confirmed this inside the CI runner.

Reproduce:
1. On a 4-vCPU machine, run `uv run --package marin-taskcompendium --group test pytest -m slow lib/taskcompendium/tests/test_evalchemy_math.py::test_minerva_concurrent_workers_complete_symbolic_matches`.
2. Or see any nightly "Marin - Unit" run since Nov 4, for example https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/43463378903 (job `slow`).

Expected: equivalent answers compare `True` when comparisons run concurrently, as the test asserts, so a busy grader does not score correct answers 0 because of parser start-up time.

The test and the bounded worker came in with #10757.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`is_equiv` sends symbolic comparisons from grading threads through `call_bounded`. The child arms a five-second wall-clock `SIGALRM` before its first LaTeX parse; under the nightly job's 48-way concurrency, time spent waiting for CPU can exhaust that alarm and is returned as `False`. The repeated CI result supports this path, though the runner has no per-worker timeout trace.

**Relevant code**
- [`minerva.py#L178-L223`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/evalchemy/scorers/minerva.py#L178-L223) — worker dispatch and alarm
- [`worker.py#L22-L49`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/execution/worker.py#L22-L49) — outer wall deadline
- [`test_evalchemy_math.py#L72-L77`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/taskcompendium/tests/test_evalchemy_math.py#L72-L77) — 48-worker regression

# Proposed Fix

`is_equiv` → `call_bounded` → `_sympy_is_equiv` currently counts scheduler delay against SymPy's five-second limit and turns that timeout into a non-match. Use a CPU-time timer for the comparison, retain the worker's 35-second wall deadline, and report an exhausted outer deadline as `GradingInfraError` so overload cannot silently assign a zero.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body: 🤖 Fix proposed in #11428. Isolated Minerva workers now count comparison CPU time, and an exhausted subprocess wall deadline raises `GradingInfraError` instead of assigning a zero. The focused safe tests pass (12/12); the 48-worker regression remains in nightly CI. The broader safe suite had 703 passes and four fixture errors because this host's Python lacks `os.pidfd_open`.

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
Queries on the Finelog `log` table that filter on `epoch_ms` open every file. The catalog does not record each segment's time range, so the time filter cannot skip any file. Most of the query time goes to reading Parquet footers, not data. That is why day-sized scans exceed the 10-second query deadline. #11087 raises that deadline to 30 seconds as a stopgap. Once time-filtered queries can skip files, the deadline can go back down.

## Evidence

A one-hour `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the `marin` hub (2026-11-08 23:38 UTC). It filtered `epoch_ms` to one hour, plus `LIKE` filters on `key` and `data`. Wall time was 7.1 s. Full query, plan and metrics: https://gist.github.com/karansag/160e31066556f7b00199c6b328d925f5

Table: `log` in namespace `marin`, 10.4 B rows, 324 GB, 1,977 segments. Trigram indexes on `key` and `data`. No sort columns and no partitioning.

| metric | value |
|---|---|
| files pruned by statistics | 1.66 K total, 1.66 K matched: **0 files skipped** |
| row groups pruned by footer stats | 2.49 K total, 6 matched |
| bytes scanned | 5.00 MB |
| `metadata_load_time` | 18.23 s |
| `time_elapsed_opening` | 52.41 s |
| output rows | 9 |

The times are summed across 16 parallel file groups, so they exceed the wall time.

The catalog records each segment's `seq` and `key` ranges, but not `epoch_ms`. So every file's footer is read just to get the `epoch_ms` min and max. After that, the query reads almost nothing: 6 row groups and 5 MB.

Impact: a 60-day pull of `levanter.model_cache` lines in 12-hour windows lost 58% of its windows to `snapshot read deadline exceeded`, even with three retries per window (#9233).

## Possible directions

- Record per-segment `epoch_ms` min and max in the catalog, so time filters drop files before they are opened.
- Sort or cluster segments by time during compaction, so those ranges are narrow.

## Done when

- A one-hour `epoch_ms` query on `log` opens only the segments that overlap that hour.
- The default query deadline can go back to 10 seconds, reverting #11087's increase.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`Store::query_providers` snapshots paths only, and `NamespaceProvider` gives every path to DataFusion before the existing row-group and index pruning runs. Neither the in-memory segment record nor the SQLite catalog carries `epoch_ms` bounds. This matches the issue's one-hour plan: 1,660 files matched file statistics, then only six row groups were read.

**Relevant code**
- [`store.rs#L515-L527`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/store.rs#L515-L527) — snapshots paths for query providers
- [`provider.rs#L112-L182`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/query/provider.rs#L112-L182) — registers all paths before scan
- [`catalog.rs#L193-L207`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/catalog.rs#L193-L207) — persisted segment columns
- [`namespace.rs#L735-L759`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/namespace.rs#L735-L759) — flush publishes segment metadata
- [`executor.rs#L318-L334`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/compaction/executor.rs#L318-L334) — compaction creates replacement metadata

# Proposed Fix

1. Measure the min/max `epoch_ms` span of current `log` segments and the overlap count for representative one-hour and one-day windows. The existing L1+ sort is by `(key, seq)`, so wide time spans could leave most files overlapping even after catalog pruning.
2. Add nullable `min_epoch_ms` and `max_epoch_ms` to the segment catalog and in-memory segment metadata. Migrate existing SQLite catalogs; derive bounds for new L0 segments from the sealed batch, carry correct bounds through compaction and level bumps, and backfill old/adopted segments from Parquet footers. A bound is usable only when every row group has complete statistics. Missing or incomplete bounds keep the segment in the scan.
3. Include bounds in the same snapshot as segment paths. For safe conjunctive `epoch_ms` comparisons, intersect the time range with those bounds and pass only overlapping paths to `ListingTable`, before DataFusion footer reads and before trigram/exact pruning. Keep the SQL predicate as a residual filter; do not infer time from `seq` or file creation time.
4. Test results and planned file groups with multiple segments, out-of-order timestamps, an old catalog, missing statistics, restart/adoption, and compaction. Benchmark the same one-hour query after backfill with maintenance quiescent. Record files opened, footer load time, and wall time; lower the raised query deadline only after representative day scans fit under 10 seconds.

No open PR found for segment time pruning. #11086 and #11087 address the deadline only. If step 1 shows most segments overlap each window, time-aware segment layout needs a separate design: changing the current `(key, seq)` layout or seq-contiguous compaction can break existing pruning and segment identity assumptions.

comments.author: HRL9000
comments.body:
🤖 **Design: in-catalog min/max bounds for declared columns, like key bounds**

This matches **proposed fix 2** in the [research comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11172#issuecomment-6773719532): per-segment `epoch_ms` bounds in the catalog, filled at write, carried through compaction and level bumps, and backfilled from footers. A segment without bounds stays in the scan. Two notes on the other fixes there:

- **Fix 1 (measure segment time spans) is done: the measurements are below.** Segments are already narrow in time: across all ~1,940 live `log` files the median spans 0.5 h, p99 8.7 h and the maximum 33 h. Replaying this issue's hour against per-file bounds keeps 2 files out of ~1,660. Details are under Background below.
- **Fix 3 is more general than the snapshot detail.** The general requirement is that the query engine uses the segments' min/max statistics correctly before opening files; carrying bounds with the segment paths is one way to do that. DataFusion can already skip files from per-file statistics it is given; today Finelog gives it none from the catalog, so it has to read every footer to find them.

The design follows. It covers background, proposal, success criteria, approach, rollout, timeframe and alternatives.

### Background and Motivation

A one-hour query on `log` is slow because Finelog opens almost every file in the table to find the few that hold that hour.

- **The query.** An `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of a one-hour `log` search opened about 1,660 files, and the `epoch_ms` filter pruned none of them. After the footers were read, only 6 row groups and 5 MB were scanned. Three hub reports for similar searches show 2,313–2,379 candidate files and 6.8–8.7 s each.
- **Why the `epoch_ms` filter pruned no file.** Before it opens files, Finelog can drop a segment by its key-column bounds, its `seq` bounds or its partition. For `log` the `epoch_ms` filter matches none of these. `log`'s key column is `key` (the log source, a string), so the catalog has no `epoch_ms` bounds, and `log` is not partitioned. The key column does two jobs, sort order and catalog bounds, and `log` chose `key` for fast per-source reads.
- **Pruning by `epoch_ms` min/max would be effective, because each file covers a short time span.** `log` has about 1,940 live files. The median file spans 0.5 h, p99 8.7 h, maximum 33 h. With per-file `epoch_ms` min/max in the catalog, the issue's hour would keep 2 files instead of about 1,660.

### Proposal

Today the catalog keeps min/max bounds for one column per table, the key column (key bounds), and query planning prunes segments by them. This proposal lets a table declare more columns that get the same in-catalog bounds. They become part of the segment list that the server keeps in memory for each table, so planning drops a segment before it opens the file, with no footer read.

- **Opt-in per column.** Bounds on every column would fit (an estimated 12–39 MB on top of about 60 MB of catalog), but most columns do not prune: each file covers nearly their full range.
- **Start with time columns.** About 65 bytes per segment: about 0.7 MB for the whole hub (about 1% of the catalog).

#### Which tables benefit

Files still opened for a window from the lookback start until now, with the share skipped:

| Table | GiB | Files | Time column | 1h | 6h | 1d | 7d | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `log` | 302.7 | 1,935 | `epoch_ms` INT64 | 62 (97%) | 69 (96%) | 103 (95%) | 169 (91%) | step 1 |
| `iris.worker` | 27.5 | 233 | `ts` | 51 (78%) | 53 (77%) | 54 (77%) | 62 (73%) | steps 1, 2 |
| `zephyr.worker` | 14.2 | 185 | `ts` | 29 (84%) | 41 (78%) | 60 (68%) | 67 (64%) | steps 1, 2 |
| `iris.task` | 11.0 | 327 | `ts` | 63 (81%) | 80 (76%) | 90 (72%) | 106 (68%) | steps 1, 2 |
| `iris.profile` | 7.7 | 155 | `captured_at` | 17 (89%) | 19 (88%) | 30 (81%) | 34 (78%) | steps 1, 2 |

- **Already pruned by time:** `levanter.metrics`, `telemetry_v1.node_agent`, `telemetry_v1.marinskyrl` and `telemetry_v1.vllm` (332 GiB). Their key is `timestamp_ms`, which is `INT64`, and the Grafana queries filter it with integer literals (`timestamp_ms >= {start_ms}`). Those filters reach the key-bound check today.
- The issue's hour was in the past, so only compacted files overlap it (2). A window ending now also keeps the 30–60 recent files that are not compacted yet, which is why the 1h column shows 62 for `log`. By bytes, the skip is 97% or more through 1d.

### Success

Success is achieved when:

1. On the hub, the issue's one-hour `log` query opens fewer than 100 files instead of about 1,660–2,370.
2. `iris.task` and `iris.worker` show the same kind of drop for one-hour `ts` filters.
3. Query results never change. The first implementation has tests that check this while bounds are absent or partial: a table where no segment has bounds yet, a mix of segments with and without bounds (as during the backfill), and the same after the backfill. Each test asserts that a time-filtered query returns exactly the rows it returns with pruning turned off.

Wall time is measured but is not a gate, because the exact cause of the 7 s is still open.

### Approach

**Step 1: bounds on `log`** (success 1 and 3)

1. Add a `catalog_bounds` column flag to the table spec, and set it on `log`'s `epoch_ms`.
2. Store each flagged column's min and max per segment in the catalog. Fill them when Finelog writes a segment.
3. Add a maintenance task that reads the footers of existing segments once and fills their bounds. Most of `log` is never rewritten, so this is needed.
4. In planning, drop a segment when its bounds do not overlap the filter's range. Always scan a segment with no bounds, so results cannot change.
5. Also read the `extract(epoch from now())` filter form that `lib/finelog/OPS.md` documents. Change `lib/finelog/OPS.md` to integer literals.

**Step 2: timestamp columns** (success 2 and 3)

6. Teach planning to read timestamp literals (`ts >= TIMESTAMP '...'`, `ts > now() - INTERVAL '1 hour'`). Planning ignores them today.
7. Set the flag on `iris.task`, `iris.worker`, `iris.profile` and `zephyr.worker`.

### Rollout

Each step deploys to `marin-dev`, then the three CoreWeave servers, then the hub. Each deploy is approved separately. Before the hub deploy, record a baseline of the issue's one-hour query.

### Expected Timeframe

- Step 1: about 1 week to a reviewed PR, then 1–2 days to deploy.
- Step 2: about 3 days to a reviewed PR, then 1 day to deploy.

### Alternatives Considered

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **Leave it in place.** Add a `seq` range to time-bounded queries. | Works today, but a user must first find the `seq` range for a time. |
| **Larger footer and index caches.** | The hub reports show 12–36 footer reads for about 2,300 files and about 7,080 index cache hits: the caches were warm and the queries were still slow. A cache also empties at each restart and must grow with the table's history. |
| **Partition `log` by time.** | Finelog has no time transform, partition selection needs exact values (`=`, `IN`), and the query side does not read a table's own partition spec. A `day` column would change every writer and query and need a rewrite of about 325 GB. |
| **Make `epoch_ms` the key column of `log`.** | The `key` bounds make per-source reads (`key = ...`) fast, which is `log`'s main read path. Keeping `key` as the sort order would need an explicit sort setting, which is part of the source layout and so rewrites the table. |

| Column | Segments | Range-filtered by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `telemetry_v1.marinskyrl.timestamp_ms` | ~3,000 | RL observability and RL runs dashboards |
| `levanter.metrics.timestamp_ms` | ~1,860 | training and runs dashboards |
| `telemetry_v1.node_agent.timestamp_ms` | ~1,360 | clusters, nodes, accelerator, capacity dashboards and the B200 utilization alert |
| `telemetry_v1.vllm.timestamp_ms` | ~1,130 | inference, inference overview, vLLM and RL observability dashboards |

`log.epoch_ms` is already flagged in #11394.

The hub's query log agrees as far as it goes. Finelog writes a `read execution report` record for every failed or cancelled read and for every successful read that takes 7 s or more. The log doesn't survive a container recreate, so it covered only about the last 2 hours:

| Table | Range filter | Outcome | Count | p50 / max | Files scanned (sum) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `telemetry_v1.node_agent` | `timestamp_ms` | ok | 4 | 8.5 / 10.1 s | 219 |
| `iris.task` | `ts` | ok | 1 | 9.4 s | 258 |
| `iris.task` | `ts` | failed at planning | 1 | 27 ms | 0 |
| `storage.usage` | none | ok | 1 | 9.6 s | 100 |
| `telemetry_v1.zephyr` | `timestamp_ms` and another column | ok | 1 | 7.9 s | 21 |

There were no cancelled reads in the window. Files scanned counts the candidate segments that reached the scan. For `node_agent` that was about 55 per query.

Left out:

- `iris.task`, `iris.task_state`, `iris.task_event`, `iris.worker`, `iris.provisioning` and `zephyr.shuffle` are range-filtered on `ts`, which is a timestamp column, and the feature covers INT64 columns only. The `iris.task` query above scanned the most files in the window, so covering timestamp columns would be a separate change worth considering.
- `telemetry_v1.zephyr.timestamp_ms` is already the key column, so key bounds already cover it. Flagging it would add nothing for its slow query above.
- `storage.usage`'s slow query has no range filter, so bounds wouldn't help it.
- Tables with fewer than about 200 segments have little to prune.

In local tests, turning the flag on for one of these tables was a metadata-only change: registering the flagged schema published a new table spec version that took effect immediately, with no rewrite of existing data. That held for unsorted, sorted, row-group-capped and partitioned object-backed tables. The production specs weren't read, and a table whose spec sets a physical layout different from its schema's own sort and row-group settings could still need a rewrite.

Two gaps remain:

- The evidence is thin: eight records from about 2 hours. A follow-up should keep these records across container recreates, so the next list can rest on a longer window.
- How much time one segment spans is not measured yet. With `seq` as the key, segments follow arrival order, so each should cover a short span. Forwarding lag and merges into the largest level can widen that.

spillover_issues.body:
🤖 **Marin Belay intake: post research ideas for [Marin Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/) here.**

Marin Belay is an agent-run experiment loop that hill-climbs the grug `fast_track` scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss).

1. **Post one idea per comment**, with a paper link or a short rationale. Add a `Track:` line to pick the baseline; the default is `speedrun` (the 8-minute d512 run). The Belay page lists the Tracks.
2. **A maintainer reviews it** on the Belay admin page and approves it for an agent session, or declines it with a reason.
3. **👀 on your comment means it has been reviewed.** Nothing else is posted here. Plans, results and decline reasons are on the Status page.

**The usual path for an idea:** optionally a `vanilla-*` Track first, for a radical idea or a stronger signal; then `speedrun`, for fast iteration and to check it fits the current recipe; then `hero-mfu` if it will change MFU a lot; then `ladder`. Maintainers promote ideas into the recipe from those results.

**Tracks** (the `Track:` line):

| Track | Runs against | Hardware |
|---|---|---|
| `speedrun` (default) | The 8-minute d512 run of the current recipe; judged at equal data, then equal time if the step time changes | 1× 8×H100 |
| `competitive-d512` … `competitive-d1280` | The current recipe at one ladder rung, compared with its finished baseline run | 8×H100; d1280 on 4 nodes |
| `ladder` | All four `competitive-*` rungs at once, at the baseline's step count. After a `hero-mfu` result, each rung's steps are adjusted for the MFU change (better MFU, more steps). Without one, the verdict is provisional: the idea needs a `hero-mfu` result before it joins the recipe | as above |
| `moe-d512` … `moe-d1280` | A basic MoE at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `vanilla-d512` … `vanilla-d1280` | A dense baseline at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `hero-mfu` | Step time of the hero GB200 stack; a maintainer runs it | 1 GB200 rack |
| `custom` | A study: runs on other Tracks, then an analysis report with no win/loss verdict; needs a node and hours budget | per study |

Wins are judged on Paloma macro loss with a noise band of 0.005 (`hero-mfu`: step time, ±0.5%).

**Example comments**

> Try warming the MuonH momentum up from 0.85 to 0.98 over the first 10% of training, as modded-nanogpt does.

> Track: moe-d768
> Replace the router's sigmoid combine weights with softmax over the top-8 experts.

> Track: ladder
> Take X0221 (CPLM Plus) up the ladder with the settings of its speedrun win.

> Track: custom
> Measure how the stable rank of each attention projection changes over a full d512 run, from checkpoints every 1,000 steps.

**The Belay app** ([public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-…](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/)):

- **[Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/):** the project. It covers the current recipe, the scaling ladder and its projection, the timeline, the gates an idea passes, the Tracks, the data and the starter kit.
- **[Status](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#status):** every idea and its results across the gates (Dense, speedrun, Hero MFU, projection, recipe), live runs and queue, and the agent log with one thread per idea (`#status/X####`).
- **[Hero MFU](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#mfu):** hero-scale throughput, with each MFU change on the GB200 stack and its branch.
- **[Admin](https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#admin)** (maintainers, signed in to Marina): review and approve or decline ideas, with instructions and node, hours and priority grants. It also sets the node cap, dispatch and GitHub reactions.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
In latentMoE, we can try initializing the up/down projections as semi-orthogonal matrices and either:

A: using an orthogonality-preserving optimizer such as the one introduced in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218 to update them
or
B: freezing them, keeping them semi-orthogonal and not updating them at all, while relying the rest of the NN to adapt

Rationale: up/down projections in latentMoE are themselves small, shared by all experts of the same layer, therefore not really having the capability to do meaningful computation for the whole NN. We should see them as information-preserving maps instead, and worry more about gradient pathology/distortion, rather than the potential loss of the degree of freedom/expressivity by using semi-orthogonal matrices.
Also if we take the "no meaningful computation" hypothesis really seriously, option B should only have negligible performance degradation compared to A. And if we use B, no new optimizer and no new hyperparameter tuning are needed.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: 🤖 Second intake test (end-to-end on main, scheduled run): this comment should be copied into #9451 within a few minutes of its 👍, then get a 🚀. Not a research suggestion.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.

Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.

But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:

1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting

And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.

The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Attention residuals q embedding:
In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from

exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))

into

exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))

q_e should be initialized as all 0.

Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Reconsider per-element attention gate, and either variant seems viable.

1. a linear projection with the same shape of the W_v projection, followed by sigmoid, like how Kimi K3 does it.
2. a down projection to a smaller vector, followed by a Swish nonlinearity, an up projection, then sigmoid, like how the current GatedNorm does it.

Rationale: the current Marin recipe has reduced the total number of MLA layers, by using a KDA+MLA hybrid, therefore the extra overhead of per-element gates compared to per-head ones becomes smaller.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):

1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.
3. RMSNorm gains that become very far away from the initial 1.
4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.

Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:

1. If we decide some of the anomalies are undesirable, we can come up with mitigations, and if the anomalies are local to some of the layers, mitigations can be local too.
2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.

These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).

Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".

Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
where y = s + r

Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.

Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.

Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.

Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body:
**Report the Paloma macro without `ptb` and `wikitext_103` next to the macro, and prefer it for calls near the bar.**

I paired each d512 Belay run (`lc1-*` in `marin_moe`) with its `-s1` twin, which has the same config apart from `trainer.seed`: 404 pairs from Sept 25 to Oct 8. These numbers are for the 305 configs near the frontier, i.e. within 0.01 of their batch median.

- **`ptb` is 1/16 of the macro but carries about a third of its seed noise** (35%). With `wikitext_103` the two carry 42%, by a covariance split.
- **Dropping the two cuts the noise much more than the signal.** Averaging the other 14 subsets cuts the noise SD of a paired Δ by 20%, while real differences between configs shrink by 3%. Signal-to-noise rises 1.4–1.5× (main estimate 1.48×, 95% CI 1.2–1.8), about what 1.5× as many seeds would buy.
- **`ptb`'s differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds:**

| Metric | Seed-to-seed correlation | Noise SD of a 2-seed paired Δ |
|---|---|---|
| Paloma macro, 16 subsets | 0.81 | 0.0016 |
| Without `ptb`, `wikitext_103` | 0.86 | 0.0013 |
| Uncheatable macro | 0.87 | 0.0014 |
| `ptb` alone | 0.10 | 0.013 |

The 0.0016 fits your "two-seed noise of ±0.004" (about 2.5 SD).

**This keeps the objective.** Near the bar, the 14-subset Δ estimates the full macro's true Δ better than the measured macro Δ does: the two-seed RMSE is 0.0009 vs 0.0011. For large changes the two can diverge, so the full macro stays the reference there.

**Two fixed-time calls** (seed 0 / seed 1):

| Call | Macro | Without the two | Uncheatable | `ptb` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Batch 174: candidate 11 vs 10 (same math, 3.5% faster) | −0.0058 / −0.0047 | −0.0075 / −0.0067 | −0.0072 / −0.0070 | +0.013 / +0.029 |
| Batch 200: candidate 12 vs 11 | −0.0001 / −0.0000 | +0.0017 / +0.0045 | +0.0043 / +0.0063 | −0.020 / −0.055 |

- In batch 174, `ptb` hid about a quarter of the gain.
- In batch 200, the exact tie was a fixed-time loss on the other 14 subsets and on Uncheatable. Its two sides ran on different clusters, but candidate 11's equal-step runs on the two clusters agree within 0.002 on these metrics.

**Why these two subsets.** They are the subsets with copies in the hero's training data (#9874), and I picked them before looking at Belay. Choosing subsets by their noise would be fitting the metric. Uncheatable works about as well.

**The bar.** You can keep 0.005 on the 14-subset Δ, for fewer false wins. Or you can lower it to about 0.004, which keeps today's false-win rate; with the observed tails the matching value is 0.0042.

Method, code and per-run numbers: https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise. I left out 6 pairs whose two seeds differ by 0.03–0.21 on the macro and by as much on Uncheatable (broken or diverged runs). Kept in, they swamp the overall variance, but the near-frontier numbers above barely move: for example, the gain is 1.38× instead of 1.48×.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
**Try numerically stable cross-entropy from [arXiv:2610.31642](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.31642).**

The paper identifies a numerical problem with standard softmax cross-entropy called **Softmax Collapse**. When the correct logit becomes sufficiently larger than the others, floating-point rounding makes its softmax probability exactly 1, zeroing its gradient while leaving non-target gradients nonzero. This breaks the zero-sum gradient invariant (the gradients across all logits should sum to zero) and can cause optimization instability, including sudden spikes in training loss.

The proposed fix is simple: exclude the correct class from the log-sum-exp calculation and use `softplus` to combine the result with the correct class's logit.

```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def cross_entropy(logits, targets):
    target_logits = jnp.take_along_axis(
        logits, targets[..., None], axis=-1
    )
    is_target = jax.nn.one_hot(
        targets, logits.shape[-1], dtype=jnp.bool_
    )

    others = jnp.where(is_target, -jnp.inf, logits - target_logits)
    return jax.nn.softplus(
        jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(others, axis=-1)
    )
```

This is mathematically equivalent to standard cross-entropy but avoids prematurely zeroing small gradients.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
Try replacing top-k routing with ReMoE’s ReLU routing and adaptive, load-aware sparsity regularization. Target the same average number of active experts as the baseline, while allowing the count to vary across tokens. Use the paper’s unnormalized nonnegative routing weights.

Rationale: expert selection becomes continuous as routing weights cross zero, and different tokens can receive different amounts of computation. ReMoe (https://arxiv.org/html/2412.14711v2) reports improved language-model loss across several scales. Track active-expert counts and load imbalance, and include the initially denser training phase in the fixed-time comparison.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
**Try adding CPLM Plus from #10678 to the Belay experiment ladder.** It extends the copy head with predecessor-conditioned keys and normalized case-class emissions, adding only d² + 2d + 1 parameters over ordinary CPLM.

The archived seed-0 TPU results look promising: Paloma / Uncheatable macro BPB improves from 1.184407 / 0.960857 to 1.181649 / 0.953552 at d512, and from 1.093305 / 0.853946 to 1.091306 / 0.850160 at d768, compared with ordinary CPLM. At d1024, Plus also improves over Belay (1.021640 → 1.014601 Paloma; 0.772050 → 0.767052 Uncheatable).

These runs approximately match analytical useful FLOPs, not wall time, and use one seed, so I think this is worth testing against the current recipe under Belay's fixed-time evaluation with paired seeds. The PR is stacked on #10260 and includes the implementation and results; throughput for the current PR revision still needs validation.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Try causal token-level capacity routing in front of the MoE (Mixture-of-Depths style ([arXiv 2404.02258](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02258)) ), keeping top-k + QB for expert choice.

Following @ClassicLarry's [comment 1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6411175364) and  [comment 2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5862159670) that dynamic compute likely matters more at scale.

Each MoE sublayer gets a small per-token router score. Tokens above a learned threshold go through the routed experts with a larger top-k; the rest go through the shared expert and the residual only. For routed tokens, expert ranking stays as in the current recipe (QB-adjusted logits, same combine weights); only k changes. Mean active experts per token matches the current recipe, e.g. with today's k = 10: 80% of tokens routed at k = 12 or 13, so the average stays ≈ 10.

Rationale: X0220 ([batch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6409675987)) showed ReMoE's failure came from the ReLU gates themselves: dead experts (40–278 per layer), 3–8% drops and load imbalance. Its allocation was already adaptive (easiest loss decile ≈ 7.4 experts, rest ≈ 12). This proposal keeps that adaptive allocation but separates the two decisions: *which tokens get more compute* (new router) and *which experts serve them* (top-k + QB, already stable here), so no expert can die from a zero gate. Mixture-of-Depths uses the same capacity idea for whole blocks.

FYI: the original MoD picks the top-k tokens over the whole sequence during training, so whether position t is routed depends on later tokens. Use a causal version instead: each token is routed by comparing its own score to a learned threshold (or a running causal quantile), with the same rule in training and eval.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Revisit MTP as a low-weight, decaying auxiliary loss computed on a subset of positions, with a block-head variant.

Batch 18 ([comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5843750617)) tried one MTP configuration: a depth-1 head (h_t + W·norm(embed(t+1)) through the shared lm_head), weight 0.3 for the whole run. 

Rationale: MTP results in the literature come from much longer token budgets, so an equal-steps vs fixed-time pair on this ladder says whether the Batch 18 loss came from the configuration or from the objective at this budget. 

Here are some things worth trying:
1. **Lower weight:** 0.05 and 0.1 instead of 0.3.
2. **Decay to zero:** linearly to 0 by 50% or 80% of training, so the late phase optimizes next-token loss only. One extra arm turns MTP off entirely after the first 50%.
3. **Block head:** replace the linear head with one lightweight Transformer block (local attention + dense FFN) that reads norm(h_t) and norm(embed(t+1)) and feeds the shared lm_head, as in DeepSeek-V3 ([arXiv 2412.19437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437)). 
Also, in a recent interview ([video, ~1:30:00](https://youtu.be/V9eI-t3TApE?t=5396)), MiMo-V2.6 leader Fuli Luo said they added MTP in pre-training because it improves the base model, and only later, while designing inference for their hybrid-SWA model, found enough spare decode compute to use MTP for speculative decoding. She also said teams that put too much faith in MLA missed this path; my reading is that MLA leaves less spare decode compute for MTP drafting. That is an inference-side hypothesis without published measurements, and I am not sure if this (spare compute) applies to our situation.
4. **(optional) Subsampled positions:** compute the t+2 logits and loss on a random 25% of positions per batch, still through the shared lm_head. If the cost scales with scored positions, the slowdown drops to about a quarter of 8.6%.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
Try adding **spelling-normalised byte embeddings** to the input. Each token's input embedding row gets a learned sum over the first 8 UTF-8 bytes of its surface string, one 256 x d table per byte position. Read the bytes after stripping leading spaces and lowercasing, so " The", "the" and "The" share every byte row. Add two small feature rows to keep what the normalisation removes: leading space (0/1) and case (lower, capitalised, all caps, mixed). Zero-init the tables so the model starts identical to the baseline. Add the byte sum to the vocab table before the token gather, so there is no per-token cost and no extra communication. Input side only: do not share byte rows on the lm_head. Keep 8 byte positions and table width d_model at every rung.

Rationale: tokens that are spelling or case variants of each other start with unrelated embeddings and have to learn their similarity from context. Sharing byte rows gives the model that information directly, and it is information the body cannot compute from token ids. This is close to Spelling Bee Embeddings (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18030); the space/case normalisation is the addition.

spillover_issues.title: Marin Belay Intake

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt-agent
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Hero (Mochi, 535B-A23B MoE) BF16 vLLM decode on GB200 is step-latency bound. Per-step time stays at 56–78 ms from 1 to 128 sequences per DP engine, so output throughput rises almost linearly with batch size until `max_num_seqs` caps it. Raising `max_num_seqs` from 32 to 64 doubles throughput at 1,024 concurrent requests (+95% to +99% in three same-node pairs, about 500 → 1,000 output tokens/s/GPU). Correctness gates pass, and latency at lower concurrency is unchanged. `max_num_seqs` 128 reached 3.6–3.8× the baseline cap at 2,048 concurrent requests (1,839 output tokens/s/GPU on a fast node set). `max_num_seqs` 256 gains nothing more, because the KV cache fills at about 250 sequences of 1K tokens per engine. With 4K outputs the KV cache fills at about 100–128 sequences per engine: 96 per engine (1,536 in flight) gives about 1,540 output tokens/s/GPU without waiting, and 128 gives 1,785–1,850 while KV-bound (R11). The `0ac9dcb` wheel from #11241 is throughput-neutral against `3004cd8` and is the current baseline. TP2 from vllm#119, a 2,048 → 8,192 prefill budget, and the one-sided NVLink all-to-all did not improve this workload.

## Description

The objective is output tokens/s per GPU under RL-rollout-like load, with time to first token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL) as guardrails. Precision stays BF16; FP8 is out of scope for now.

Setup for every measurement below:

- Weights: the SFT checkpoint `step-400407` exported as BF16 safetensors (export schema 3), `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/exports/mochi-sft/hero-sft-fullab-step393k-v2/step-400407/2af3f828aa-cpu-a1` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fexports%2Fmochi-sft%2Fhero-sft-fullab-step393k-v2%2Fstep-400407%2F2af3f828aa-cpu-a1)). Router and experts are stored in placed order `1e80fa529585`.
- Serving: Marin vLLM fork release `marin-vllm-gpu-20261113-0ac9dcb157ee`, the #11241 pin (`3004cd8f1632` before it was accepted).
- Topology: one 4-node GB200 gang (16 GPUs) in one NVLink domain on cw-us-east-08a, TP1 / DP16 / EP16, all-to-all `allgather_reducescatter`, Triton MoE, FlashInfer attention.
- Batching and context: `max_num_seqs` 32, `max_num_batched_tokens` 2,048, prefix caching off, `max_model_len` 262,144, one API server.
- Compilation: PIECEWISE CUDA graphs with `splitting_ops` = `unified_attention_with_output`, `unified_kv_cache_update`, `grug_moe_short_conv`.

This is the same configuration as the team's BF16 serving endpoint for the checkpoint (`hero-sft-step400407-bf16`). Its batch-1 decode reproduces that endpoint's logged ITL: 56 ms here against 58 ms.

Load: 1,024 GSM8K test questions with the Marin chat template (mean prompt 70 tokens), temperature 1.0, a fixed seed per request, `ignore_eos`, 1,024 output tokens per request. The loop is closed: the generator keeps a fixed number of requests in flight, three waves per point. Throughput is the output-token rate from when all in-flight requests have produced their first token until the last submission, divided by 16 GPUs. A batch-1 point (8 × 256 tokens) gives single-request latency.

Each candidate runs on the same 4 nodes as its control, back to back in one job. GB200 node sets on the cluster differ by about 20% in throughput for identical software, so unpaired comparisons are not used.

Frozen inputs: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/inputs/cases-0baf4938.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Finputs%2Fcases-0baf4938.json)). Per-run outputs (`gates.json`, `long.json`, `load.json`, vLLM logs): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/runs/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Fruns%2F)). These prefixes expire 14 days after writing. Code: research branch [`mcwitt/vllm-hillclimb`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/mcwitt/vllm-hillclimb), `experiments/evaluation/hero_vllm_hillclimb/` (multi-host DP serving on Iris, probes, grading, JAX reference). Each result was produced from a committed tree: R0 at [`a300d1a588`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/a300d1a588), R1a/R1b/R2a/R3 at [`9adfa3d7a1`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/9adfa3d7a1), R2b/R4/R5/R6 at [`e8cc54609b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/e8cc54609b), R2c/R4b/R7/R8 at [`a2b182ff87`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/a2b182ff87), and the JAX reference at [`d8a9890cea`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/d8a9890cea).

## Correctness gates (v4)

The JAX reference is Levanter scoring the same `step-400407` checkpoint in placed order: BF16 weights, fp32 log-softmax, zero dropped MoE assignments, and a router bias that matches the export to 2.4e-7. It covers 11,370 positions in 32 fixed histories (GSM8K chat prompts and book excerpts, 40–1,835 tokens), plus 4K, 32K and 65K book histories (last 512 positions and every 256th). Outputs: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=14d/hero-vllm-hillclimb/reference/ref-a4/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D14d%2Fhero-vllm-hillclimb%2Freference%2Fref-a4%2F)).

- (a) Hard: prompt scoring on DP engine 0 is bitwise identical across three passes within one server instance: alone, while the other 15 engines decode 8 requests each, and alone again.
- (b) Hard: the per-position maximum probability error of vLLM's top-5 against the JAX top-64 stays inside the control band for p50, p90, p99 and the fraction above 0.075, on both the short histories and the long histories. The band is the union of per-run 95% bootstrap intervals (whole histories resampled) over 5 control runs. Band, short histories: p90 [0.018, 0.034], p99 [0.066, 0.114], fraction above 0.075 [0.7%, 2.5%]. Band, long histories: p90 [0.022, 0.026], p99 [0.049, 0.069].
- (c) Decode non-regression against the control, distributional.
- (d) The decode load-dependence defect below is measured for every candidate. A change in it is called only after repeats.
- CUDA graphs must be captured; a run aborts if vLLM resolves `cudagraph_mode` to NONE.

An absolute 0.075 maximum is not used. At 11,370 positions the control itself reaches 0.50 at near-tie positions. Cross-run bitwise equality is also not used: fresh compiles of an unchanged config differ (see below).

## Results

"In flight" is the number of requests the server is processing at once (the closed-loop concurrency of the load generator, across all 16 GPUs). It is not a context length. Every row uses the same sequences of about 1,100 tokens (a 70-token prompt plus 1,024 sampled output tokens), except R10 and R11, which generate 4,096 output tokens. Throughput is output tokens/s per GPU. Each candidate ran back to back with its control on the same 4 nodes.

Decision rule: a candidate is decided on output tokens/s per GPU at 1,024 requests in flight (2,048 for the `max_num_seqs` 64 → 128 step and for the KV-bound 4K rows; 512 for rows that were swept only to 512). A change counts as a gain only beyond ±2%, the spread measured between same-node pairs that should be equal (the wheel pairs and the `max_num_seqs` pairs at 512 in flight). Latency columns are guardrails. Verdict words: "gain accepted" improves the deciding metric; "adopted, neutral" was taken for another reason with no measurable throughput effect; "no effect"; "rejected".

R0 is the mean of the `max_num_seqs` 32 controls measured on fast node sets, with the range and run count. No `max_num_seqs` 32 control was measured at 2,048 in flight on a fast node set, so that cell is blank.

A 262K measurement needs three things: a long-context load (prompts up to 262,144 tokens, for example the AgentX traces in #11320), parity cases at 131K and 262K, and a JAX reference job sized for them. The 65K reference already peaked at 141–155 GiB/GPU on 4 nodes. KV capacity is about 1.0M tokens per engine, so at most 3 full-length sequences fit per engine at this layout.

## Known defects

- Open: decode is not invariant to load on other DP engines. Engine 0 decodes the same prompts alone, then while the other 15 engines are busy. Only 1–2% of its decode steps keep a bitwise-identical top-1 log-probability. Top-1 |Δp| reaches p90 0.013–0.016 and max 0.09–0.11 (0.16–0.20 nats); greedy tokens flip, once at a 0.43-nat margin. Load on engine 0 itself gives the same size of change. Repeated runs alone are bitwise identical, and prompt scoring (prefill) under peer load is bitwise identical. Both wheels show it. Inferred mechanism, not traced: DP lockstep pads every engine to the per-step maximum token count, which changes GEMM shapes and BF16 rounding.
- Fresh compiles of an unchanged config produce different numerics. Five compiles of `3004cd8` fell into three groups. Within a group, scoring is bitwise identical. Between groups, scoring differs at 99.5% of positions (|Δp| p99 0.072–0.075, max 0.48–0.56). The distributional statistics against JAX barely move: short-history p90 0.0270–0.0273, p99 0.0871–0.0885. Kernel autotuning or benchmarking at compile time is the suspected cause. Disabling Inductor's combo-kernel benchmarking did not remove the modes (R8), so the cause is still open.
- A Hero launch whose `--compilation-config` omits `vllm::grug_moe_short_conv` from `splitting_ops` runs without CUDA graphs. The fork's ShortConv guard sets `cudagraph_mode` to NONE with only a log line. Batch-1 decode was 182 ms/token against 56 ms with graphs.
- Open: three Triton kernels compile during serving instead of at startup (seen in the baseline and `0ac9dcb` server logs): `_causal_conv`, `fused_moe_kernel` and `_topk_log_softmax_kernel`. Inferred, not measured: the first requests that reach them pay the compile time.
- Two GB200 node sets ran about 18–25% slower for both wheels: s76txs64, s9jtxs64, s7xsxs64, s8ltxs64 (rack 125) and s7psxs64, s96txs64, sbftxs64, sb3txs64 (rack 124). The cause is undetermined.
- vllm#119 at `ef7f5a0` (the TP2/TP6 numbers in #11320) predates vllm#121, the position-dependent query scaling that export schema 3 requires. A merge onto `0ac9dcb` needed three fixes: allow Hero TP for schema 3, apply the TP2 NCCL guard to schema 3, and reshape Q by the per-rank head count in log scaling. Without the last, TP>1 crashes.

## Open questions

- The KV cache, not per-step time, caps the batch (R7): about 220 sequences per engine at 1K tokens and about 97 at 4K, from the fork's block accounting (4 attention groups at 16 tokens per block, with sliding-window groups holding every token below 2,048, plus 12 ShortConv state blocks). Fork changes could add about 12.5% (store 6 global KV heads instead of 12) and about 3% (ShortConv page padding). The 4K-output runs (R10, R11) matched the model: KV use was 31.7% at 32 sequences per engine and 47.2% at 48, and the cache filled with 96–128 sequences running per engine.
- The load generator stays below one core up to 4,096 requests in flight; four API servers lower TTFT but not throughput (R4b).
- The log-scaled query scaling starts at 65,536 tokens. The 131K and 262K parity cases are not run yet.
- Throughput on long-context agentic traffic, where TP2 may help (#11320).
