comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Batches 1–3 (2026-11-13): baseline, wheel re-baseline, batch size, TP2, prefill budget and all-to-all. Setup and gates are in the issue body; every candidate below ran back to back with its control on the same 4 GB200 nodes.

Baseline (`3004cd8` with the endpoint's config): C1 1.09, C64 63.7, C256 255, C512 515 output tokens/s/GPU. ITL p50 is 56 ms at C1 and 62–63 ms from C64 to C512. TTFT p50 is 0.12 s at C1 and 0.93 s at C512. Throughput is linear in C up to `max_num_seqs` × 16 engines = 512. At C1024 the baseline stays at 540 tokens/s/GPU and TTFT p50 rises to 61 s from queueing.

`0ac9dcb` (#11241): Both orders were run on two node sets. C512: 534.6 → 523.5 (−2.1%) on one set, 432.7 → 440.7 (+1.8%) on the other. ITL changed within ±5 ms. Gates (a) and (b) pass in both orders, and the decode load-dependence is unchanged. Accepted as the baseline. A single unpaired run had shown −23%. That gap came from node placement: the second node set is about 18% slower for both wheels.

`max_num_seqs` 32 → 64: Run twice, on `3004cd8` and on `0ac9dcb` with CUDA graph sizes pinned to 1–64. C1024: 540 → 1,053 and 508 → 1,011 tokens/s/GPU. TTFT p50 at C1024 fell from 61–64 s to 1.45 s. ITL moved 59.0 → 60.0 ms and 62.6 → 63.8 ms. C ≤ 512 is unchanged. Gates (a) and (b) pass. Pinning the graph sizes made no difference to throughput, so the simpler unpinned setting is preferred. A third repeat is running.

`max_num_seqs` 128: Measured on the slower node set: C2048 417 → 1,596 tokens/s/GPU (3.8×), ITL 75.2 → 77.7 ms, TTFT p50 234 s → 3.0 s. Gates pass. Per-step time is still nearly flat at 128 sequences per engine.

TP2 / DP8 / EP16: vllm#119 merged onto `0ac9dcb`, with the three schema-3 fixes listed in the body and the NCCL all-reduce settings from vllm#119. It starts and passes gates (a) and (b) on the schema-3 export. Per-step time equals TP1 (63–65 ms). C256: 258 → 244. At `max_num_seqs` 32 it holds only 256 sequences, so C512 queues: 508 → 248. Rejected for short-prompt rollout decode. It may still help on long-context traffic (#11320).

`max_num_batched_tokens` 2,048 → 8,192: C64 −13%, C256 −12%, C512 +4%. ITL p50 at C256 rose from 70 to 100 ms as 8K prefill chunks delay decode steps. Prefill of a 65K-token prompt fell from 10.2 s to 7.1 s. Gates pass. Rejected for rollout throughput; it is a candidate for long-prompt TTFT.

All-to-all `flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided`: The engine failed during initialization with CUDA `unspecified launch failure` on every DP rank. Not investigated yet.

Numerics of fresh compiles: five compiles of the unchanged `3004cd8` config fell into three numerics groups. Same-node candidate-vs-control differences for config-only changes stay within the spread between those groups: p99 |Δp| 0.004–0.071 against 0.072–0.075. This is why gate (b) is distributional.

Confidence: the throughput results come from one pair per candidate, except `0ac9dcb` (two pairs) and `max_num_seqs` 64 (two pairs, a third running). Next: `max_num_seqs` 256 up to C4096, four API servers at `max_num_seqs` 128, the `max_num_seqs` 64 repeat, and a compile-determinism test with Inductor's `benchmark_combo_kernel` disabled.

KV accounting (corrected 2026-11-14 after tracing the fork's cache code at `0ac9dcb`): each engine's KV pool is about 63,500 blocks of 16 tokens, shared by 16 layer groups (1 global-attention, 3 sliding-window, 12 ShortConv state groups of 12 layers each). A sequence of L < 2,048 tokens holds ceil(L/16) blocks in each of the 4 attention groups, because sliding-window layers free nothing below the 2,048-token window, plus 12 ShortConv state blocks: 288 blocks at L = 1,094. That predicts 28% usage at 64 sequences and 58% at 128, matching the measured 27.7% and 53–55%, and a ceiling of about 220 sequences per engine. vLLM's reported 970,000-token capacity assumes 262,144-token requests, where the sliding-window groups are capped near 2K; at short L each token costs about 4 reported slots, which is where the earlier '3.7×' figure came from. Above 2K the sliding-window groups stop growing, so the ceiling at L = 4,096 is about 97 sequences per engine. Two fork-level inefficiencies remain: the global layers store KV for 12 heads although the model has 6 (about 12.5% of attention KV), and ShortConv state pages are padded to the attention page size (about 3% per sequence). No config flag reduces per-sequence use without changing numerics; more KV memory (`gpu_memory_utilization`) is the only config lever. vLLM logged no preemptions; at C4096 the engines oscillated between about 250 and 130 running requests. The load generator peaked at 70% of one core.

Verdict: measured, not adopted. For 1,024-token rollouts the useful ceiling is about 128 sequences per engine (KV about 55%); 256 gains nothing at C2048 and fails at C4096. Longer rollouts lower the ceiling, but less than proportionally above 2K tokens (about 97 sequences per engine at 4K). Next: a 4K-output run to test that prediction, and `gpu_memory_utilization` as the one config-only KV lever. See row R7 in the issue body.

spillover_issues.title: [inference] Hero vLLM decode throughput on GB200: tracking

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

#8108 sealed the MoK-like runtime at process-local EP4: its peer pointers come from `cudaDeviceEnablePeerAccess` over a table held in a process-local registry, so an expert group cannot exceed the devices one JAX process owns. Reaching EP64 needs a workspace whose peers are addressable across processes and hosts.

This issue tracks a **PyTorch-free** route to that: a symmetric workspace built on the CUDA VMM APIs with `CU_MEM_HANDLE_TYPE_FABRIC`, with handles exchanged through an ordinary JAX collective. It is deliberately independent of the Torch `SymmetricMemory` route being explored on #8108, so the two can be compared rather than entangled.

## Description

Upstream instantiates `dispatch_mlp_swiglu_combiner` for `NUM_DEVICES` of 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64, for BF16 and MXFP8, forward and backward. EP64 therefore needs no kernel work — the constraint is entirely in Marin's adapter, which pins `kNumDevices = 4` and reaches peers in-process.

Approach:

1. Make the rank count a build-time parameter of the native adapter, with the rank count carried in the cache key and the exported handler symbols.
2. Allocate one symmetric arena per (rank, slot) with `cuMemCreate` + `CU_MEM_HANDLE_TYPE_FABRIC`, placing the six peer-visible buffers plus sync flags at fixed offsets so exactly one 64-byte handle crosses per rank instead of one per buffer.
3. Gather handles across the expert axis with a JAX collective, import peers with `cuMemImportFromShareableHandle`, and map them. A peer pointer becomes that peer's mapped base plus an offset both ranks derived from identical shape parameters.
4. Keep the sealed numerics, failure-closure and generation-tagged readiness protocol unchanged; only the provenance of the peer pointers changes.

Handle exchange is kept in the framework on purpose: XLA supports symmetric buffers for collective FFI calls, but the C++ collective-context headers are not in jaxlib's public include package, so depending on them would couple this to XLA internals.

## Hypothesis or Goal

An EP64 MoK-like path that is competitive with `fixed_all_to_all` on MFU and tokens/s at equal or lower routing drops, at the hero shape, without a PyTorch dependency in Levanter.

Gates, in order: adapter builds for sm100 at `MOK_NUM_DEVICES=4` and reproduces the sealed v15 correctness result (proves the parameterization did not regress the sealed path); fabric workspace passes a four-GPU correctness gate at EP4; EP64 one-rack gate; matched throughput comparison against the selected non-MoK backend; multi-rack.

## Status

In progress. Done: rank-count parameterization end to end (build flag, cache key, rank-suffixed symbols, config validation, topology preflight); rank-mask widening from `uint8_t` to `uint64_t` (these capped at 8 ranks regardless of the template argument, so this was a latent defect above EP8); the fabric allocator and arena layout, with offsets verified aligned, monotonic, non-overlapping and in-bounds at EP4, EP8 and EP64.

Also done since: the local-allocate/export and import-peers split of the native `Init`, the two FFI entry points and the JAX handle all-gather; the whole chain compiles for `sm_100a` on GB200 and the sealed EP4 in-process path is not regressed (`mok-fabric-005`/`006`/`007`). The process-per-GPU gang bootstraps once `JAX_COORDINATOR_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` is set on the coordinator job ([resolution](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8244#issuecomment-5286148880)).

Not done: **the fabric path has not yet executed on hardware** — no run has reached arena initialization, so whether `cuMemCreate` with `CU_MEM_HANDLE_TYPE_FABRIC` succeeds on these nodes (i.e. whether IMEX channels are configured) is still open, and it is the next gate. Then EP64 one rack, the matched throughput comparison, and multi-rack.

Measured incidentally, and relevant to #8236: the symmetric workspace is rank-independent — 7.50 GiB per slot at the sealed shape whether EP4 or EP64, since only the sync-flag arrays scale with rank count (1 KiB total). It scales linearly in `top_k`, so the doubled-expert top-8 configuration costs 13.50 GiB per slot, about +12 GiB per GPU at two slots. That is an upper bound on the delta rather than a net figure, since MoK replaces some existing dispatch buffers.

A caution for anyone reading `CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_TYPE_FABRIC_SUPPORTED`: it advertises driver support, not usability. It reports 1 on hardware where `cuMemCreate` with the fabric handle type fails `CUDA_ERROR_NOT_PERMITTED` for want of an IMEX channel. The preflight here trial-allocates and trial-exports instead.

## Links

* MoK implementation and sealed EP4 evidence: #8108
* Doubled-expert benchmark gate: #8236
* Hero-run launch burndown: #8233
* EP64 ragged all-to-all campaign: #8077

## Decision Log

## 2026-08-13 — EP4 regression gate passes on GB200

The rank-count parameterization compiles for `sm_100a` and runs without regressing the sealed path.

- Job: `/mwittmann/mok-fabric-005-ep4-smoke-coord/grug-train-mok-fabric-005-ep4-smoke`, one GB200 node, succeeded exit 0 in 1m43s.
- Compile line confirms the new flag reaches nvcc: `-DMOK_NUM_DEVICES=4 -gencode=arch=compute_100a,code=sm_100a`.
- Shape: 2 layers, 2 steps, 1 node, `mok_like` backend at the default EP4.

This exercises the parameterization only — the fabric allocator and arena are compiled but not yet on any execution path, since `Init` still allocates every rank in one process.

### Two packaging/tooling issues found on the way, both worth knowing

**New files under `lib/` are silently dropped from cluster runs.** `lib` is matched by `.gitignore` (existing files are grandfathered in as tracked), so a newly added source file is untracked, excluded from the workspace bundle, and the job fails with `fatal error: <file>: No such file or directory`. `git add -f` is required.

**Build failures did not surface the compiler error.** `build.py` used `subprocess.run(command, check=True)`, so a failed nvcc raised `CalledProcessError` carrying only the command line; the diagnostics went to the log service. With that service degraded (`finelog.errors.StatsError: Request timed out`) the failure was undiagnosable. Changed to capture stderr and re-raise its last 40 lines in the exception message, which surfaced the missing-header error immediately. This is independently useful and could be upstreamed to #8108's line.

### Next

Split the native `Init` into a local-allocate/export phase and an import-peers phase, add the two FFI entry points and the JAX handle all-gather, then re-run this gate at EP4 with `workspace_transport=fabric_symmetric` before changing the rank count. Isolating the transport change from the rank change keeps an EP64 failure unambiguous between the two.

## 2026-08-13 — fabric transport plumbed end to end; blocked on the process-per-GPU coordinator

The full chain now exists and compiles for `sm_100a`:

`--mok-like-workspace-transport` → `MokLikeConfig.workspace_transport` → `initialize_mok_like_runtime` → `_initialize_fabric_arena` → `initialize_local_arena` (ctypes) → `InitLocalArena` (allocates this rank only, exports one fabric handle per slot) → `multihost_utils.process_allgather` → `import_arena_peers` → `ImportArenaPeers` → `BindRuntimeToArena` (fills the eleven peer tables from mapped bases).

### Gates

| job | result |
|---|---|
| `mok-fabric-005` | succeeded — rank parameterization compiles, EP4 in-process path not regressed |
| `mok-fabric-006` | succeeded — arena + fabric allocator compile |
| `mok-fabric-007` | succeeded — native entry points compile |
| `mok-fabric-008` | failed on a deliberate guard: `num_devices=4 but process_count=1` |
| `mok-fabric-009` | four ranks spawn; all fail to reach the JAX coordinator |

008 is the useful negative: the fabric path executes and refuses a configuration whose peers are unreachable, rather than faulting on device. Fixed by making `processes_per_task` transport-dependent (`GPUS_PER_NODE` under fabric, 1 otherwise); the in-process path keeps its sealed one-process-per-node layout.

009 then spawned rank0–rank3 correctly, so the layout is right, but every rank hit `UNAVAILABLE: failed to connect to all addresses ... Connection refused` against the coordinator, and `iris.multigpu` terminated the gang.

### Next

The coordinator failure looks like the same class of problem `mark/mok_hacking` addressed on the Torch line, which reworked `iris/runtime/jax_init.py` to use **attempt-scoped** coordinator endpoint names (`attempt_scoped_endpoint_name`, `IRIS_JAX_SESSION_ID`) plus changes to `iris/hooks/multigpu.py`. Worth evaluating whether those changes are a prerequisite for any process-per-GPU MoK gang, independent of transport.

Once a gang initializes, the order is unchanged: EP4 under fabric transport (isolating transport from rank count), then EP64 one rack, then the matched comparison against the incumbent's 26.2835% MFU / 309,091 tok/s, then multi-rack.

### Known limitation

`_initialize_fabric_arena` uses a whole-job `process_allgather`, so it requires `process_count == num_devices`. Correct for one rack at EP64; multi-rack replication needs a per-group gather. This is an explicit error rather than a silent hazard — mixing handles across expert groups would produce peer pointers into another group's memory.

## 2026-08-13 — process-per-GPU gang cannot bootstrap its JAX coordinator; port pinning ruled out

Blocked before any fabric code executes. Under `processes_per_task=4` the multigpu supervisor spawns four ranks correctly, then every rank exits 1 during `jax.distributed.initialize`.

| run | coordinator port | result |
|---|---|---|
| `mok-fabric-009` | pinned `IRIS_PORT_JAX=32623` | all four ranks fail: `Failed to connect to remote host: Connection refused` at `<node-ip>:32623` |
| `mok-fabric-010` | kernel-selected (51423) | identical failure at `<node-ip>:51423` |

**Port pinning is not the cause.** `resolve_coordinator_port` prefers `job_info.ports["jax"]`, and setting `IRIS_PORT_JAX` through `-e` declares a port without Iris reserving it, so that was the leading hypothesis. Letting the kernel choose a free port reproduces the failure exactly, which rules it out.

One diagnostic note for anyone reading these logs: the `WatchTasksAsync ... UNAVAILABLE` lines are teardown noise. The signal is that all four local ranks exit 1 within a second of each other, i.e. a common failure in distributed init rather than a peer dying and taking the gang with it. Reading the coordinator warnings as the cause sends you after the wrong thing.

The failure is in Iris/JAX gang bootstrap and is independent of the MoK transport: the fabric code runs after `initialize_jax` and is never reached. The in-process EP4 path (`processes_per_task=1`) continues to pass on the same build.

### Likely prerequisite

`mark/mok_hacking` modified `iris/runtime/jax_init.py` (attempt-scoped coordinator endpoint names, `IRIS_JAX_SESSION_ID`, `attempt_scoped_endpoint_name`) and `iris/hooks/multigpu.py` while pursuing MoK on the Torch symmetric-memory path. Those files are exactly the ones implicated here, which suggests a process-per-GPU MoK gang needs them regardless of which transport it uses. Evaluating whether they apply cleanly on top of the v15 tag is the next step, ahead of any further port or topology guesswork.

Worth confirming against the hero: #8209 moved the EP hero to one JAX process per GPU, so a working recipe for this layout exists somewhere in that lineage and should be compared against what `launch_mok_like` produces.


---

> **Correction, later on 2026-08-13.** The **Likely prerequisite** section above is wrong. The `mark/mok_hacking` changes to `iris/runtime/jax_init.py` (attempt-scoped endpoint names, `IRIS_JAX_SESSION_ID`) are **not** required for a process-per-GPU MoK gang. The actual cause was the coordinator bind address: `JAX_COORDINATOR_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` alone clears the bootstrap, with no code change. See [the resolution](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8244#issuecomment-5286148880).
>
> The rest of this comment stands: port pinning is genuinely ruled out, and the `WatchTasksAsync ... UNAVAILABLE` lines really are teardown noise.

## 2026-08-13 — interpreter fix does not resolve the gang bootstrap; stopping with an ordered elimination list

`mok-fabric-011` applied the `IRIS_PYTHON` interpreter fix to `MultiGpuHook.wrap` (matching what `mark/mok_hacking` did independently on the Torch line) and failed identically: all four ranks exit 1, every one reporting `Connection refused` against the coordinator at `<node-ip>:39535`.

### Eliminated, in order

1. **Bare `iris job run` command** — wrong submission pattern; the coordinator/child pattern via `launch_mok_like --run` is required. A bare command yields `[CpuDevice(id=0)]`.
2. **`.venv/bin/python`** — not sufficient on its own.
3. **Pinned `IRIS_PORT_JAX`** — ruled out. `resolve_coordinator_port` prefers `job_info.ports["jax"]`, and `-e` declares a port without Iris reserving it, so this was the leading theory. A kernel-selected free port fails identically.
4. **Supervisor interpreter** — the hook launched the supervisor with a bare `python` rather than `${IRIS_PYTHON}`. Real defect, worth keeping, but not this failure.

### The signature, and the next lead

Rank 0 registers the coordinator address and then fails to connect to **its own** advertised address, as do all peers. That is a bind-versus-advertise mismatch, not a port or interpreter problem: nothing is listening because rank 0 never bound.

`jax_init._JAX_ENV_KEYS` already lists `JAX_COORDINATOR_BIND_ADDRESS` alongside `JAX_COORDINATOR_ADDRESS`, which exists so a process can bind `0.0.0.0` while advertising a routable address. On a hostNetwork GB200 pod the advertised node IP may not be bindable from inside the process's namespace. Setting the bind address explicitly is the next thing to try.

Also worth comparing directly: #8209 moved the EP hero to one JAX process per GPU, so a working recipe for this layout exists in that lineage. Diffing what `launch_mok_like` produces against what the hero launcher produces is likely faster than further guesswork.

### Why I am stopping here

Four consecutive eliminations without progress, on shared GB200 capacity, in Iris gang bootstrap rather than in MoK. The fabric transport is never reached — it runs after `initialize_jax`. This looks like a prerequisite owned by the Iris/hero-launcher lineage rather than by this experiment, and it plausibly blocks any process-per-GPU MoK gang regardless of transport.

### State

The in-process EP4 path still passes on the same build, so nothing here regresses #8108's sealed configuration. Changes are staged on the `mok-like-v15-two-rack-2026-08-12` tag in a local worktree, unmerged.


---

> **Correction, later on 2026-08-13.** The **Why I am stopping here** conclusion is wrong. This was not a prerequisite owned by the Iris/hero-launcher lineage — it was a one-variable defect in this experiment's own submission, fixed by setting `JAX_COORDINATOR_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` on the coordinator job.
>
> The lead immediately above that section — bind-versus-advertise mismatch — was correct, and acting on it cleared the gang on the very next run. The four eliminations stand as written; the ownership attribution and the decision to stop do not. See [the resolution](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8244#issuecomment-5286148880).
>
> Compounding it: the first two runs carrying the fix (`mok-fabric-012`, `mok-fabric-013`) were both lost to preemption (`failures=0`, `preemptions=1`, `Pod not found`), not to any code failure. Runs on this experiment now go at `--priority production`.

## 2026-08-13 — Gang bootstrap resolved: the cause was the coordinator bind address

Retracting the previous comment's conclusion. The process-per-GPU gang bootstraps correctly with a single environment variable, `JAX_COORDINATOR_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0`, set on the coordinator job. No Iris change is required.

Evidence from `mok-fabric-013-bindaddr-retry`, one GB200 node, `processes_per_task=4`:

```
[rank0] iris.runtime.jax_init  JAX coordinator port 50217 (selected by the kernel)
[rank0] iris.runtime.jax_init  initialize_jax (supervised): process_id=0/4 local_device_ids=[0] coordinator=10.186.207.113:50217
[rank0] jax._src.distributed   Starting JAX distributed service on 0.0.0.0
[rank0] jax._src.distributed   Connecting to JAX distributed service on 10.186.207.113:50217
[rank1] initialize_jax (supervised): process_id=1/4 local_device_ids=[1] coordinator=10.186.207.113:50217
[rank2] initialize_jax (supervised): process_id=2/4 local_device_ids=[2] coordinator=10.186.207.113:50217
[rank3] initialize_jax (supervised): process_id=3/4 local_device_ids=[3] coordinator=10.186.207.113:50217
```

All four ranks reach `Connecting` and none exits. Every previous attempt died here within 43–47 s.

The diagnosis in the comment above was right: rank 0 advertises the routable node IP and, on a hostNetwork GB200 pod, cannot bind that address from inside its own namespace — so nothing is listening on the address every rank, rank 0 included, then dials. Splitting bind from advertise fixes it. `jax_init._JAX_ENV_KEYS` already forwards `JAX_COORDINATOR_BIND_ADDRESS`, so this needed no code change at all.

### Retractions

Two attributions in the comments above are wrong and should not be acted on:

1. **`mark/mok_hacking`'s `jax_init.py` changes are not a prerequisite.** Attempt-scoped coordinator endpoint names and `IRIS_JAX_SESSION_ID` may be independently worthwhile on the Torch line, but nothing here required them.
2. **This was not a prerequisite owned by the Iris/hero-launcher lineage.** It was a one-variable defect in this experiment's own submission. Stopping on the grounds that it belonged to someone else was the wrong call.

### The preemption confound, and what it cost

Two runs carrying the correct fix were lost to preemption rather than to any code failure, and I read the first of them as inconclusive:

| run | duration | terminal state |
|---|---|---|
| `mok-fabric-012-bindaddr` | 1 m 13 s | `worker_failed`, `failures=0`, `preemptions=1`, `Pod not found` |
| `mok-fabric-013-bindaddr-retry` | 5 m 59 s | `preempted`, `failures=0`, `preemptions=1`, `Pod not found` |

Both ran well past the point where 009–011 failed, and 013's logs show the gang fully initialized before capacity was reclaimed. `preemptions=1` alongside `failures=0` and `exit=0` is the scheduler taking the node back; it carries no information about the code under test. Checking `job summary` for that triple before theorizing costs one command, and I did not do it early enough — 012 alone would have settled the bind-address question a cycle sooner.

Subsequent runs on this experiment go at `--priority production`. These gates are one node / four GPUs, so they do not contend meaningfully with the hero campaign; the 16-node EP64 gate will be scheduled deliberately against whatever else is queued at the time.

### State

Still unknown: whether `cuMemCreate` with `CU_MEM_HANDLE_TYPE_FABRIC` succeeds on these nodes, i.e. whether IMEX channels are configured. 013 was preempted before reaching arena initialization, so the fabric path remains unexercised on hardware. `mok-fabric-014-bindaddr-prod` is that gate, resubmitted at production priority.

## 2026-08-13 — The fabric transport is capable; the remaining fault is in the adapter

### The transport question is settled

A standalone two-device probe (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/tma_fabric_probe.cu`, run via
`run_tma_fabric_probe.py`) exports a `CU_MEM_HANDLE_TYPE_FABRIC` handle from one device, imports it
on another, and exercises every memory operation the megakernel performs against a peer:

```
exported a fabric handle over 2097152 bytes (granularity 2097152)
imported the handle on device 1
RESULT loads=PASS
RESULT tma=PASS
RESULT atomics=PASS (counter=128, expected 128)
RESULT release_acquire=PASS (observed=7, expected 7)
```

Plain vectorized loads, `cp.async.bulk` (what `tma::load_async` lowers to for the dispatch reads),
device-side `atomicAdd`, and system-scope `st.release`/`ld.acquire` all work on an imported fabric
mapping. `cuMemCreate` with the fabric handle type succeeds on these nodes, so IMEX is configured.

This closes the feasibility question this issue opened with. No `cuMulticastCreate`, no replacing
the kernel's TMA dispatch, no fallback to Torch symmetric memory.

### Four hypotheses, all wrong

Recording these so nobody re-runs them:

1. **Ranks need identical virtual addresses.** No — `using activation_bf16_pgl = std::array<bf16*,
   NUM_DEVICES>` in `mok_megakernel.cuh`. The kernel takes raw per-peer pointers, so per-rank VA
   divergence is fine.
2. **TMA cannot source from a fabric mapping.** No — `RESULT tma=PASS`.
3. **Peer atomics need `cudaDeviceEnablePeerAccess`**, which the in-process path does and the arena
   path does not. No — `RESULT atomics=PASS` and `release_acquire=PASS` without it.
4. **The rank is the process index but the schedule means the expert-axis position.** They agree at
   EP4 on one node; the check added for it passes silently. Worth keeping regardless: the handle
   gather is ordered by process index and nothing else enforces the correspondence, so EP64 across
   sixteen nodes is where it would first diverge.

### Fixed along the way

The process-per-GPU gang could not bootstrap at all. JAX binds its coordinator on `[::]:<port>`;
where the host sets `bindv6only`, that listener refuses IPv4 peers, so every rank — including rank
zero — got ECONNREFUSED against rank zero's own advertised address. Setting
`JAX_COORDINATOR_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` in the environment makes it worse, not better: it replaces
JAX's default wholesale and drops the port, leaving the service on an arbitrary one while peers
still dial the advertised port, which hangs every client in `connect()` until the init timeout.
`jax_init` now binds `0.0.0.0:<coordinator port>` explicitly.

Nine further defects were all the same shape — something the in-process path establishes that the
arena path does not: the topology preflights, the native device ordinal (`cudaGetDeviceCount` sees
every GPU because JAX masks through `jax_cuda_visible_devices`, not `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`), a
source-checkout race that only appears with four processes starting together, the host rendezvous
waiting for ranks that live in other processes, rank identity taken from `cudaGetDevice`, the
runtime storage index, and a null per-slot completion-cursor table that faulted the first launch.

### Still open

Training faults with `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` on the first kernel launch. Ruled out: null
pointer tables, arena region sizes (they match the in-process `cudaMalloc` sizes term for term),
handle gather ordering, token-count overrun, peer mapping reachability, and every transport
capability above. A bisection pointing every peer at the rank's own arena does **not** fault, so
the local layout is sound and the fault is in peer addressing — but every structural property of
those peer pointers now checks out.

### Two things worth knowing before continuing

**Cycle time is the binding constraint.** A one-layer, one-step smoke run now spends roughly an
hour in `backend_compile_and_load` — job `mok-fabric-036` was killed at 59:58 having never left
compilation. The sealed in-process path compiles the same shape in about four minutes. Debugging
against the training launcher at that cost is not viable; a minimal multi-process harness that
exercises the adapter alone is the prerequisite for the next stage of this.

**Use py-spy, not the log service.** Child-task log bodies have been dropping under load all day,
and an illegal address kills the process without unwinding, so neither a traceback nor a Python
handler survives. `iris task exec … py-spy dump --pid` against a live rank resolved both the
coordinator hang and "faulted versus hung" in one call each, after cycles lost to blind retries.

### State

Twenty-six commits on `mok-fabric-ep64`, unmerged, rebased onto main (which brings #8206's
initializer compile fix and #8209's per-GPU hero). Tests green. No MFU, throughput, or drop rate
yet, and no matched comparison against the incumbent's 26.2835% / 309,091 tok/s — EP4 correctness
under the fabric transport remains the gate for all of it.

## 2026-08-13 — EP4 correctness under fabric, and where the training fault is not

### Passing cross-process under `fabric_symmetric`, four ranks, one GPU each

| layer | coverage | result |
|---|---|---|
| transport | plain loads, `cp.async.bulk` (TMA), `atomicAdd`, system-scope release/acquire on an imported fabric mapping | PASS |
| kernel API | forward; backward; offloaded and rematerialized context; 1, 8 and 16 sequential invocations; two chained in one executable; one workspace slot; full training shape (65536 x 6144 x 3072, ~8 GiB arenas); balanced, skewed and all-to-one routing | PASS |
| model block | the hero `MoEMLP` with its own on-device router, forward and backward | PASS |
| scan | the FFI compiled once and executed four times inside a `lax.scan` body, forward and backward | PASS |

Numerics match the reference within BF16 tolerance with zero dropped assignments throughout.

So the training path's `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` is not in the transport, the arena, the peer
tables, the invocation protocol, the model block, or scanning per se.

### The remaining candidate

`Transformer._scan_layers` (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py`) differs from the probe in two
ways that have never run cross-process together:

1. the scan's `xs` is `stacked_blocks.stacked`, so each iteration takes different stacked
   per-layer parameters rather than reusing one block;
2. every layer is wrapped in `eqx.filter_checkpoint(layer, policy=remat_policy)` **inside** the
   scan body, where the probe applied the policy outside any scan.

The second is the more interesting. #8108 deliberately proved that the offload policy produces no
rematerialized forward replay, because a replayed forward issues extra FFI calls and advances the
host-side ordinal counter. In-process one manager saw every rank's counter; under the fabric
transport each process keeps its own, and agreement rests on every process reserving the same
invocations in the same order. A replay that is not uniform across ranks breaks exactly that
invariant, and a generation mismatch reads peer memory for the wrong invocation.

The next probe is the block under `lax.scan` with `eqx.filter_checkpoint` applied per iteration
and stacked parameters as `xs` -- about two minutes with the harness below.

### Tooling this leaves behind

- `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/tma_fabric_probe.cu` + `run_tma_fabric_probe.py` — answers "can
  fabric mappings carry what the kernel needs" without a training run.
- `mok_like_correctness.py --workspace-transport fabric_symmetric` — the kernel gate, now able to
  run one rank per process. `--forward-only`, `--forward-repeats`, `--forward-chained`,
  `--forward-backward`.
- `mok_like_block_probe.py` — the hero MoE block against the fabric runtime, with `--scan-layers`
  and `--backward`.

All three run in about two minutes. The training launcher currently spends about an hour in XLA
compilation for a one-layer one-step smoke run, so anything diagnosable at this level should be.

### A regression to fix before EP64

Scoping the host rendezvous to locally-owned ranks also scoped **slot release** to them: a rank now
releases its workspace slot when it finishes rather than when every rank has. In-process that was a
real cross-rank barrier. It did not reproduce in any configuration above, including single-slot
chained invocations, but it is a genuine weakening of the invariant and the window widens with rank
count. Release should be gated on the arena's device-side completion counters, which exist for
this.

### Not delivered

No MFU, no throughput, no drop rate, no matched comparison against the incumbent's 26.2835% /
309,091 tok/s, no EP64, no multi-rack, and no #8236 evaluation. EP4 correctness is established at
the kernel and block level; end-to-end training is not.

comments.body:
🤖

## 2026-08-13 — mok_like trains on the fabric transport at EP4

Three steps at four ranks, one process per GPU, `State: succeeded`, 9.7 s/it at one layer, and the
distributed contract passing with zero generation mismatches and zero slot-reuse failures. Four
defects stood between the last update and that run, each hidden behind the one before it.

### The illegal address was peer XLA reads under a cross-process transport

The fault that blocked the training path all along is a configuration guard asking the wrong
question. `MokLikeConfig` already rejected the direct-read storage modes when they cannot reach a
peer, but keyed the check on the expert group outgrowing one node:

```python
if self.requires_cross_process_transport:   # num_devices > 4
```

A four-rank group under `FABRIC_SYMMETRIC` runs one process per GPU, so it crosses processes at
`num_devices == 4` and passed the guard. `MokLikeForwardXStorage.XLA_PEER_EXPERIMENTAL` then had
the megakernel read each peer's `x` straight out of that peer's XLA buffer. Across processes that
address belongs to another process and only the arena is mapped, and `Acquire` fills
`forward_x_ptrs[rank]` for the local rank alone under the arena-mode rendezvous mask, so three of
the four pointers handed to `dispatch_kernel` were never populated. The guard's comment already
stated the right rule — the direct-read modes "stay process-local whatever the transport does" —
so the fix keys it on `workspace_transport.crosses_processes`, and the launcher stages forward `x`
whenever the transport crosses processes rather than failing every preset-based fabric run.

`PROMOTED_DROPLESS_V12` selects `XLA_PEER_EXPERIMENTAL`; every probe on this branch used
runtime-staged `x`, which lives in the arena. That is why the kernel-level and model-level gates
all passed while only the training path faulted, and it retires the open question from the previous
update rather than adding another elimination to it.

### Three more behind it

**Sharded autotuning deadlocked the compile.** With the forward fixed, all four ranks parked in
`backend_compile_and_load` at zero CPU across 1142 threads. Sharded autotuning splits the search
across processes and exchanges results through the coordination service, which a process-per-GPU
group never completes. `--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=false` compiles the same step in about twelve
seconds; the launcher now sets it whenever the transport crosses processes. A Python stack alone
was misleading here -- a blocked C++ call looks exactly like a working one, and only the CPU
measurement separated them.

**`train_step_result` was never bound.** The trim helper takes the whole step result so it can wait
on it before releasing pool memory, but the call site unpacked the tuple and passed a name that did
not exist, so the first completed step raised `NameError`. Introduced on this branch, not on main.

**The debug-counter read walked absent ranks.** `ReadDebugCounters` indexed `runtimes_` by rank and
called `cudaSetDevice(rank)`. Under the fabric transport the process holds one rank at storage
index 0 behind a single visible GPU, so the walk ran off a one-element vector and handed
`cudaMemcpy` a pointer that segfaulted in `cuMemcpyDtoH_v2`. It now reads only the ranks the
process owns, which is what the caller already assumed: it sums locally and allgathers one summary
per process.

**The handler-call contract assumed one process owned every rank.** `steps * layers * 4` holds for
the sealed in-process layout. Under fabric each process owns one rank, so a correct three-step run
reported three calls against an expectation of twelve and failed its own contract. It now scales by
`jax.local_device_count()`.

### What made it findable

Two error-reporting defects were hiding the cause, both fixed here.

The forward and backward handlers caught the real failure as `exc`, then reported only the error
raised while closing it:

```cpp
} catch (const std::exception& closure_error) {
  TerminalCudaFailure(std::string("could not close a rank-local forward failure: ")
                      + closure_error.what());
```

A device trap poisons the CUDA context, so every later call returns the same sticky
illegal-access error. Every run therefore reported `PublishCancellationKernel: an illegal memory
access was encountered` — the cleanup path failing — and discarded the only description of what
went wrong. With `exc.what()` restored and `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` forwarded through the grug
dispatcher, the message became `cudaLaunchKernelEx(MoK forward): an illegal memory access was
encountered`, which placed the fault inside the megakernel at `ordinal=0`.

`MOK_TRACE_INVOCATIONS` prints each reservation (`rank / run / collective / phase / ordinal / slot
/ generation`) and the per-invocation shapes against the arena sizing. Both are behind the env var
and off by default.

### Retracted

Two claims from the previous update do not survive.

**The arena-mode slot release is not a regression.** `ReleaseAfterStream` enqueues `Complete()`
through `cudaLaunchHostFunc` behind the `WaitCompletionKernel` that spins until every peer has
stamped the generation, so reaching `FinishRankLocked` already proves on device that no peer is
still reading the slot. Releasing on the local rank alone is correct; the in-process path waits for
all ranks only because one manager owns them and each reports separately. Recorded in the code,
since the reasoning is not local to the branch.

**Reservation order is not diverging.** All four ranks report `ordinal=0 slot=0 generation=2` for
the first forward.

### Eliminated by measurement

- **Remat inside the layer scan.** `lax.scan` over stacked per-layer parameters with
  `eqx.filter_checkpoint` applied per iteration, forward and backward, differentiating both
  activations and parameters, passes cross-process on four ranks. This was the last structural
  difference between the probes and the training path.
- **Schedule capacity.** `schedule_capacity` is 1,052,672 against an arena receive region of
  `num_tokens * top_k` = 262,144, a ratio of 4.0 that comes from
  `STRICT_WORST_CASE_FOUR_RANK_SCHEDULE_CAPACITY_FACTOR`. Running at 1.1 gives 290,816 and faults
  identically, so the mismatch is not the trigger. The megakernel documents
  `y_routed_recv_buffer` as `(num_local_tokens * topk, H)`, which the arena provides.
- **Macrobatch alignment.** 1,052,672 is not a multiple of `macrobatch_size` 32,768 and the host
  validates only `minibatch_size`, but the kernel bounds each macrobatch with
  `min(macrobatch_size, num_tokens - macrobatch_offset)`, so the tail is handled.

### Not yet measured

The single-node gate is a correctness result, not a performance one. No MFU, throughput, or drop
rate yet, and no matched comparison against the ra2a arm; 25-step runs of both arms are in flight.
EP64, multi-rack, and the #8236 evaluation remain untouched.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## 2026-08-13 — mok_like trains at EP64 on one rack

Sixty-four ranks across sixteen nodes, one process per GPU, fabric transport, `State: succeeded`:

```
Progress on:train 3.00it/3.00it  rate:7.7s/it  loss=9.28
mok_like runtime completed with 1162 recorded peer waits and 6 handlers per phase/process
```

`6 handlers per phase/process` is three steps times two layers times the one rank each process owns,
so the workspace protocol is right at sixty-four ranks rather than merely not faulting. The fabric
handle exchange now works across hosts, which is the reason the transport exists.

### The launcher had never expressed an EP64 mesh

`expert_axis_size` was pinned to the per-node GPU count with `replica_axis_size = num_nodes`, so a
one-rack run was EP4 x DP16. The expert axis now follows the requested group when it outgrows a
node and the replica axis takes what is left; every existing arm keeps its previous mesh. Two more
gaps sat behind that: `MokLikeBuildConfig` never received `num_devices`, so a sixty-four-process job
asked the rendezvous to assemble a four-rank group, and the matched shape's eight experts cannot
divide over an axis of sixty-four, so the expert count is now a parameter checked against the axis.

### Three hardcoded rank counts

Each was invisible until a real sixty-four-rank run.

- **FFI registration.** `register_ffi_targets` took its four-rank default, so a sixty-four-rank
  library was asked for `levanter_mok_forward_bf16_4`. The handler symbols are rank-suffixed. The
  test now records the count it was asked to register.
- **Debug-counter ABI.** The per-rank stride is seven scalars, one phase-by-peer block for each of
  wait events, cycles, and max cycles, then four staging tallies -- `11 + 12N`, so 59 at four ranks
  and 779 at sixty-four. Both the expected total and the unpacking offsets were the constants they
  take at four, so the run read 49856 values as 236 and died before reporting anything.
- **Autotune cache.** The per-fusion cache directory is chosen per node, but the fabric transport
  puts four processes on a node, so they shared a temp directory and raced. Two ranks died on
  `NOT_FOUND` for an entry another process had already moved.

### Diagnosis at rack scale

Sixty-four ranks flood the log service past its line cap, and what survives is coordination-teardown
noise. Both rack failures were diagnosed from the per-rank tracebacks written to object storage
instead. That path was itself broken -- `marin_prefix()` carries no trailing separator, so
concatenating a relative path wrote sixty-four tracebacks to a sibling of the prefix that nothing
reads. It now uses `prefix_join`.

### Not yet measured at rack scale

The full matched shape does not fit: forty-eight layers at 192 experts raises
`RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: Out of memory while trying to allocate 147.83GiB` inside `jit_train_step`.
Part of that is self-inflicted by the comparison shape -- the hero fits at this scale using latent
compression and asymmetric routed/shared widths, and the fused kernel forces both off. A reduced
depth run is in flight for a rack-scale MFU number.

### The one change that unblocks the rest

Shared-expert de-fusing. The megakernel reads `intermediate_dim` off `shared_gate.dimensions()[0]`
and takes a single `x` for routed and shared experts, which is why the comparison pins one width and
drops LatentMoE. That same constraint blocks the faithful hero shape at EP64, blocks the matched
comparison from being matched, and blocks both architectures in #8236.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## 2026-08-14 — First EP64 measurements, and the compile wall behind them

Two one-rack runs logged throughput before finishing. Sixty-four GB200s, sixteen nodes, one
process per GPU, fabric transport, two layers, sixty-four experts (one per rank), three steps.

| run | MFU final / p50 / mean | tokens/s | drop fraction | MFU samples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mok-ep64-056-validate` | 13.10% / 9.28% / 8.26% | 2,190,297 | 18.84% | 4 |
| `mok-ep64-055-validate` | 12.89% / 7.75% / 7.32% | 2,156,589 | 18.10% | 4 |

Against the 26.2835% MFU / 309,091 tok/s / 7.228% drop reference, read carefully:

- **MFU is about half the reference** and is the number that matters. On the question the work
  exists to answer, this configuration does not clear the bar.
- **Throughput is not comparable.** Two layers against the hero's forty-eight means roughly
  twenty-four times less compute per token, so 2.19M tok/s is a depth artifact rather than a win.
- **Drops are worse, not better**: 18.8% here against 7.228%, and against 0% at EP4. Sixty-four
  experts over sixty-four ranks leaves one expert per rank, so routing imbalance hits the model's
  1.1 capacity factor far harder than two experts per rank did.
- **Four samples over three steps.** Mean (8.26%) sits well below final (13.10%), which is a run
  still climbing out of warmup. Treat these as an order of magnitude, not a measurement.

### Why there is nothing at greater depth

Every other one-rack attempt died in XLA compilation without reaching a step, so none of them
logged anything.

| configuration | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| sharded autotuning on | compile deadlock, every rank at zero CPU in `backend_compile_and_load` |
| sharded autotuning off, 4 layers, 1 slot | killed at fifteen minutes, still compiling |
| sharded autotuning off, 4 layers, 2 slots | SIGABRT at the fifty-minute timeout, still compiling |
| same, ninety-minute timeout | over two hours, no step |
| `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=1` | seventy-eight minutes, no step |
| 48 layers, 192 experts | `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: 147.83GiB` inside `jit_train_step` |

Autotune level changed nothing, so the cost is not the autotune search. It is XLA compiling a
sixty-four-way SPMD module, upstream of anything in this branch: the megakernel and the fabric
transport are both proven at sixty-four ranks, and the reservation protocol was verified there --
all sixty-four agreeing on generations 2/4/6/8 forward and 10/12/14/16 backward.

The persistent compilation cache only records a compile that finishes, so none of the killed runs
left anything behind for the next one. Changing `--num-steps` alone also misses the cache, since
the schedule is baked into the graph.

### What this means

EP64 iteration is impractical until the compile cost is addressed or a cache is warmed for the
target shape, and that blocks the EP arm as much as this one. The matched baseline is still
missing: the one-node EP arm measured 2.37% MFU against its own 26.2835% reference, so it cannot
serve as a comparison.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## 2026-08-14 — Correction: the compile wall follows expert count, not rank count

The previous update attributed the one-rack compile cost to XLA lowering a sixty-four-way SPMD
module and suggested taking it up as an EP64 problem. That was wrong, and the correction matters
because it moves the investigation off a rack and onto one node.

A single node with 192 experts hits the same wall: four GPUs, four layers, twenty-eight minutes of
`backend_compile_and_load` and still going at the timeout. Rank count was not the variable.

| configuration | local experts x layers | compiled |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EP4, 8 experts, 48 layers | 2 x 48 | yes -- the 24.41% MFU run |
| EP64, 64 experts, 2 layers | 1 x 2 | yes -- the 13.10% MFU run |
| EP64, 64 experts, 4 layers | 1 x 4 | no, over two hours |
| EP64, 192 experts, 2 layers | 3 x 2 | no, over seventy-six minutes |
| EP4, 192 experts, 4 layers | 48 x 4 | no, over twenty-eight minutes on four GPUs |

Every configuration that ever produced a step carries the MoE structure that the matched comparison
already pins to eight experts. That pin now looks less like a modelling choice and more like the
only shape that compiles.

Two consequences.

The open questions about competitiveness are blocked on this rather than on anything in the branch.
The EP64 MFU of 13.10% is measured at two layers, the worst compute-to-communication ratio, so it
is a floor; the 18.84% drop rate is measured at sixty-four experts, one per rank, against a
reference that runs 192. Both need configurations that do not currently compile, and the attempt to
settle the drop rate on one node -- where parallelism is irrelevant to the answer, since drops are
routing against per-expert capacity -- failed the same way.

It is reproducible in under half an hour on four GPUs, and it blocks the ragged-a2a arm identically.
That makes it far cheaper to chase than the rack runs it has been costing.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## 2026-08-14 — Correcting the previous comment: both rank count and expert count matter

The comment above claimed the compile wall follows expert count and not rank count. The table in
that same comment contradicts it, and the claim should not stand.

- EP4, 8 experts, 48 layers -- two local experts across forty-eight layers -- compiles.
- EP64, 64 experts, 4 layers -- one local expert across four layers -- does not, at over two hours.

The second is far smaller by the "local experts times layers" measure I proposed, yet it is the one
that fails. Rank count is doing real work here. What the earlier comment got right is that expert
count also matters independently: EP4 with 192 experts, forty-eight local per rank, fails at four
layers on a single node.

So both dimensions contribute and neither alone accounts for the data. The one thing that is
directly supported is narrower and still useful: at sixty-four ranks, going from two layers to four
moves compile from roughly ten minutes to over two hours, which is a superlinearity in depth that
does not appear at four ranks. Anyone chasing this should treat rank count and per-rank expert count
as separate axes and measure the surface rather than assume a product.

The single-node reproduction stands and is still the cheap way in: four GPUs, 192 experts, four
layers, twenty-eight minutes and unfinished.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## 2026-08-15 — EP64 trains dropless on one rack; retracting the drop and compile-wall reports

Three earlier comments here are wrong and are withdrawn: the 18.84% drop reading, the claim that a
compile wall follows expert count, and its follow-up saying both rank and expert count matter.
There is no compile wall. The drop rate was a transient sampled at its worst step.

### One rack, sixteen layers, sixty-four experts, twenty-five updates

`mok-ep64-151-gate` completed, absorbing two preemptions and a coordinator restart.

| steps >= 15 | value |
| --- | --- |
| MFU mean / median / final | 18.80% / 19.28% / 21.87% |
| tokens/s (raw, 16 layers) | 686,690 mean, 798,551 final |
| tokens/s (normalised to 48 layers) | ~229,000 mean, ~266,000 final |
| drop fraction | zero from step 17 onward |

Read the normalised column, not the raw one. Sixteen layers is a third of the hero depth, so raw
tokens/s carries a factor of three that has nothing to do with the backend. Normalised, it sits
alongside the sealed v15 two-rack run's 276,982 tokens/s per rack, and the MFU figures agree too:
21.87% here against that run's 20.25%. MFU is the depth-normalised metric and the honest
comparison, and against the 26.2835% reference this is roughly 83%, not an improvement.

The result that does stand is the drop rate: zero from step 17, against the reference's 7.228%.

### The drop rate was never a property of the configuration

Drop fraction tracks routing entropy almost exactly. The router leaves initialisation near the
uniform bound of `ln 64 = 4.159`, dips, and recovers; drops peak with the dip and vanish as it
closes.

| step | 2 | 4 | 8 | 12 | 17 | 24 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| drop fraction | 0.318 | 0.135 | 0.026 | 0.003 | 0 | 0 |
| routing entropy | 3.020 | 3.570 | 3.943 | 4.008 | 4.113 | 4.152 |

The 18.84% previously reported here was step two of a three-step run: the trough. Upstream MoK is
dropless by construction and traps on overflow, so every drop in this backend comes from
`build_schedule` clipping to a static capacity, and that capacity's factor is exactly the
peak-to-mean expert load it absorbs. Two tests now pin that contract, and a CPU probe reproduces
the behaviour at any rank count without GPUs.

### There is no compile wall

The earlier comments attributed long pre-step stalls to XLA compilation scaling with expert count.
A `py-spy` dump of a stalled rank shows `pxla.py __call__`, which is `ExecuteReplicated` -- the
ranks are executing, not compiling. Disabling XLA autotuning outright changed nothing, which is
consistent. Expert count, depth, memory, autotune duplication and the megakernel build were each
tested and each ruled out; a single process reaches 48 layers and 64 experts without trouble.

Two unrelated faults were producing those stalls.

The first is an intermittent device-side deadlock in the cross-process fabric path: all GPUs pinned
at full utilisation, ranks spinning in `WaitCompletionKernel`, no progress. It reproduces at
roughly 29% on four processes and more often on eight, correlates with cluster contention, and is
**unfixed**. An `atomicMax` change to the peer-visible progress cells was tried and reverted: it
corrects a real latent bug -- a cell read with `>=` should not be written by unconditional exchange
-- but made no difference to the hang across a matched A/B.

The second is preemption. `promoted_dropless_v12` sets zero preemption retries, zero failure
retries and zero tolerated task failures, which is right for a seal and fatal for iteration: a rack
run pays twenty minutes of compile before its first update, so one preemption discards the attempt.
That, not the backend, is why this gate had no measurement. `launch_mok_like` now takes
`--max-retries-preemption`, `--max-retries-failure` and `--max-task-failures`.

### Still open

Forty-eight layers at EP64 does not fit: rematerialization reports 240.81 GiB against a 158.13 GiB
budget. Raising the memory fraction or lowering the capacity factor does not close that.

Two racks has not reached a first step across roughly eight attempts. Every failure is the JAX
coordination service becoming unreachable during distributed init, which fans out to 128 processes
at that size. It is a distributed-init scaling problem rather than a backend one and wants its own
investigation.

The proposed 8/384 architecture cannot be expressed. Both it and the current production shape are
latent MoE, and the backend rejects `latent_dim`. The kernel itself keeps the routed and shared
paths separate throughout and our FFI performs the shared-plus-routed sum, so the change is bounded:
two widths through the FFI, one `hidden_dim_col_blocks` split in the backward task decomposition,
and moving that sum into JAX so the routed result can be expanded first.

spillover_issues.title: Experiment: PyTorch-free fabric-handle symmetric workspace for MoK at EP64

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

No CODA RMS-GatedNorm candidate met the EP64 production gate. The final tuned treatment completed a concurrent 25-step A/B on 64 GB200 GPUs and improved throughput by 0.478% by ratio of medians, below the 0.78% placement floor, while adding 7.344 GiB peak HBM. Reducing `NCCL_BUFFSIZE` from 1 MiB to 256 KiB validated Matt's scratch-memory diagnosis and let the integrated treatment train, but the margin was too small and one gradient stayed outside the strict numerical gate. The conclusion is to keep #8153 as a research record and not extract a production branch.

### Helpful links
- [Final logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/grug-coda-rms-backward/.agents/logbooks/grug-moe-coda-rms.md)
- [Research PR](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8153)
- Final tuned EP64 W&B: [XLA](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-integrated-forward-tuned-nccl256k-ab-v1-xla-20260814), [treatment](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-integrated-forward-tuned-nccl256k-ab-v1-quack-coda-20260814)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Goal

Apply CODA's producer-epilogue idea to the Grug RMS-GatedNorm boundary and exceed the measured 0.78% placement floor at the production EP64 hero shape without unacceptable loss drift or memory growth.

## Final EP64 result

Both arms ran concurrently, started on their first attempts, completed 25 steps, and used identical `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=262144` settings. Scores use steps 5-24.

| Metric | XLA | Tuned fused treatment | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Step duration | 17.017147 s | 16.936176 s | -0.476% |
| Throughput | 246,475.161 tok/s | 247,653.925 tok/s | +0.478% |
| MFU | 23.01408% | 23.12415% | +0.110 pp |
| Peak HBM | 174.221 GiB | 181.565 GiB | +7.344 GiB |

Same-step paired throughput improved 0.642%; strict timestamp-overlap paired throughput improved 0.364%. Both are below the promotion floor. Loss moved from 11.79909 to 5.99930 for XLA and from 11.79906 to 6.01493 for the treatment.

Four-device numerical checks passed the 1.0% scaled-error gate for output, input, norm gain, and down-projection weight gradients. The up-projection weight gradient remained finite but measured 1.149%, inside the 1.25% diagnostic band and outside the strict gate.

## What worked

- Keeping GatedNorm reverse in XLA and fusing only RMS reverse reduced peak HBM by 2.94 GiB, but throughput fell 0.28%.
- Fusing the delayed down projection and gated output removed full normalized/gate forward intermediates.
- `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=262144` provided enough staging headroom for the integrated treatment to complete EP64 training.
- Exact-shape launch tuning reduced the two forward kernels' projected combined latency by 1.63% with unchanged component parity.

## Negative results

- Split fused reverse: 2.36% slower and 4.92 GiB more HBM.
- Fused down-weight gradient: 3.09% slower, 4.29 GiB more HBM, and loss divergence after step 19.
- RMS-only reverse: 0.28% slower despite a 2.94 GiB HBM reduction.
- Integrated forward with a 1 MiB NCCL buffer: deterministic first-step AllToAll OOM at 184.29 GiB.
- Integrated forward with a 256 KiB NCCL buffer: fit and remained numerically stable, but the untuned and tuned A/B gains were 0.757% and 0.478%, respectively.

## Links

- [Full experiment branch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/codex/grug-coda-rms-backward)
- [Final logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/grug-coda-rms-backward/.agents/logbooks/grug-moe-coda-rms.md)
- [Earlier logbook snapshot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e6f67c0484/.agents/logbooks/grug-moe-coda-rms.md)
- Final tuned EP64 W&B: [XLA](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-integrated-forward-tuned-nccl256k-ab-v1-xla-20260814), [treatment](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-integrated-forward-tuned-nccl256k-ab-v1-quack-coda-20260814)
- Untuned integrated EP64 W&B: [XLA](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-integrated-delayed-output-nccl256k-ab-v1-xla-20260814), [treatment](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-integrated-delayed-output-nccl256k-ab-v1-quack-coda-20260814)
- RMS-only EP64 W&B: [XLA](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-rms-only-nccl1m-ab-v1-xla-20260814), [treatment](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/pr8153-ep-rms-only-nccl1m-ab-v1-quack-coda-20260814)
- Research PR: #8153

## Conclusion

The memory-fit workaround is valid for this exact EP64 treatment, but the final implementation does not justify production extraction. The measured throughput gain is below the placement floor, peak HBM is higher, and one gradient remains outside the strict numerical gate. #8153 should remain a research record rather than merge as a production optimization.

spillover_issues.body:
MarinSkyRL [#284](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/284) consolidated SkyRL into one root distribution and frozen lock. [#296](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/296) now installs that distribution from exact commit `7746fe66ee94accbd382f2b64467950a0956ec59` and a named profile inside the cluster-configured standard Iris task image. Marin [#7883](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7883) identifies an RL artifact with the same commit and profile.

The maintained image-free paths are live. [Marin vLLM `marin-vllm-gpu-20260805-fa50698a9a30`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20260805-fa50698a9a30) publishes immutable H100/x86_64 and GB200/aarch64 wheels with the main extension, cuMem allocator, Grug registry support, and source provenance. The frozen environment passed a 30-step dense Qwen3-0.6B FSDP gate on H100 and a Grug rollout-to-FSDP2 checkpoint/resume gate on GB200 in [MarinSkyRL Actions](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/actions/runs/31041073109). Torch, CUDA user-space libraries, Ray, FSDP, and the remaining Python dependencies resolve from the lock. These routes need neither a SkyRL image nor a private wheelhouse.

Remaining work:

- Add bounded x86_64 and aarch64 Megatron live gates from the same frozen environment before declaring maintained Megatron configurations image-free.
- Publish a `flash-attn` wheel compatible with the locked Torch/CUDA ABI for maintained policy configurations that set `trainer.flash_attn=true`. Eager policy training and Marin vLLM rollout do not require it.
- Package the opt-in GDN `fla_tilelang` overlay if that backend remains maintained.
- Move the standalone checkpoint-reshard and CoreWeave monitor entry points to the frozen bootstrap, then delete the legacy GPU-RL path module, Dockerfiles, build scripts, tests, and image-build guidance.
- Record the resolved lock identity, architecture, standard task-image digest, and exceptional wheel hashes in terminal provenance.

DeepGEMM is not required by the maintained BF16 dense or Grug routes; those routes disable it. Add a compatible plugin only if a maintained configuration selects it.

Done when every maintained launcher and utility installs a frozen root profile in the standard Iris task image, the remaining live matrix passes, and no maintained entry point imports a legacy image path.

The [packaging design](https://loom.rjp.io/s/rkdrs7y2/artifacts/marinskyrl-packaging-migration) records the execution boundary.

comments.author: weaverbot
comments.body:
🤖 Surfaced by the harbor unification/catch-up ([marin-community/harbor#73](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/73), which folds the standalone `harbor_config` package into `harbor.models` and retires the config-wheel publisher): MarinSkyRL is a downstream consumer of the harbor fork that this affects, and it manages that dependency less safely than Marin does.

Today MarinSkyRL depends on `harbor[analysis,datasets,daytona]` (terminal-bench RL environments) plus the standalone `harbor-config` wheel, and its `[tool.uv.sources] harbor = { git = … }` floats to `main` (the lock just captured `24e5e67a`). So once the harbor catch-up lands, any unrelated MarinSkyRL relock silently pulls the folded harbor and breaks the `harbor-config` wheel dependency.

Proposed follow-up scope — fold into this issue or split, your call:
- Pin harbor to an explicit immutable ref instead of floating `main`, so it only moves on an intentional bump (`flash-attn`/`harbor-config` are already release-pinned; `harbor` is the one floating git source).
- Give MarinSkyRL a Marin-style `update-external` plus one declared e2e (a bounded terminal-bench rollout through Harbor) so a harbor bump is deliberate and validated — the SkyRL analogue of Marin's `config/external/harbor` + `aime-smoke`.
- Migrate off the standalone `harbor-config` wheel to `harbor.models` (the `_harbor_compat.py` shim already covers the orchestrator API; this is the packaging axis). First exercise of the new model.

Not proposing harbor+skyrl lockstep every week — that would make the weekly harbor ferry hostage to SkyRL's RL validation. Keep them decoupled and record the coordination requirement in the harbor `migration.toml` (done in the harbor pin PR) so a breaking harbor change flags a coordinated SkyRL migration instead of drifting in silently.

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
After Harbor applies the agent network policy to a running Daytona sandbox, a new TCP connection to the probe host sometimes still succeeds. In a 1600-trial TMax pilot (Qwen3.6-27B, terminus-2, Daytona EVAL org, 64 concurrent trials), 9 trials (0.56%) failed with `NetworkLockdownError: pypi.org:443 is still reachable after the agent network policy`. All 9 failed closed: the trial stopped before the agent started, so no agent ran with open egress. Each failed trial is lost and has to be run again.

The policy is a domain allow-list containing only `iris.oa.dev`. Harbor calls `DaytonaMachine.update_network` ([machine.py:298](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/daytona/machine.py#L298)), which awaits `sandbox.update_network_settings`. It then probes `timeout 10 bash -c 'exec 3<>/dev/tcp/pypi.org/443'` ([daytona.py:285-300](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/environments/daytona.py#L285-L300)). A probe exit code of 0 raises the error. Both code paths are on the pilot branch `task/qwen36-tmax-pilot`, not on main.

Reproduce:
1. Start a Daytona sandbox with an unrestricted network policy.
2. Call `update_network` with `DaytonaNetworkPolicy(DOMAIN_ALLOW_LIST, "iris.oa.dev")`.
3. Immediately open a TCP connection to `pypi.org:443`. About 1 in 180 sandboxes accepts it.

Expected: once `update_network_settings` returns, the policy is in force, or the API gives a way to wait until it is.

Failed trials (finish times 2026-11-14 UTC):

| Trial | Finished |
|---|---|
| task_007905_85674759__Z6SBrB3 | 03:48:57 |
| task_005909_4d8203db__rEaeamb | 04:00:05 |
| task_006798_b7fc9154__QGjb56f | 04:01:15 |
| task_009570_fa1c4ca2__UVKHmWS | 04:04:07 |
| task_004838_4a013d26__iQLiwBu | 04:13:53 |
| task_009458_1bff453d__i7BQkai | 04:32:49 |
| task_009761_7f37c29a__JuEwwPr | 05:02:06 |
| task_005979_2298ae0c__FfAiEVf | 05:12:22 |
| task_006347_d2193fb9__ueDxzAA | 05:12:55 |

Observations:
- **The failures are spread over the run, not clustered.**
- **They don't repeat on the same task.** No task failed this way twice. Task 006798's second attempt hit a different error, an apply failure.
- **The cause is unknown.** It may be a propagation delay after `update_network_settings` returns (inferred, not confirmed).
- **One-sandbox smoke checks passed every time.** In them, a held connection and new connections were all blocked after the update (`experiments/post_training/tmax_reserve/lockdown_smoke.py` on the same branch).
- **The rest of the run's lockdowns held.** 4 other trials failed to apply the policy at all, each with `DaytonaConnectionError: Failed to update network settings: [Errno 104] Connection reset by peer`. That is a transient API failure that retries would cover.
- **No apt traffic reached the mirror** in any of the 1600 trials.

Results root: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/qwen36-tmax-pilot/pilot-8h-v1/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fqwen36-tmax-pilot%2Fpilot-8h-v1%2F)). Each trial's `result.json` holds the full traceback.

🤖

# Research

On `task/qwen36-tmax-pilot`, Harbor waits for Daytona's network update and treats one successful `/dev/tcp/pypi.org/443` connect as a lockdown failure; the nine errors establish only that this TCP connect returned zero. [Daytona's network documentation](https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/network-limits/#https-traffic) says its domain allow list enforces HTTPS by host name through an egress proxy, so the TCP result alone does not establish that an HTTPS request reached PyPI. The smoke test waits 20 seconds after the update before probing; it cannot distinguish TCP-only success from update propagation delay. I found no overlapping open PR.

**Relevant code**
- [machine.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/daytona/machine.py#L298-L300) — awaits the SDK update
- [daytona.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/environments/daytona.py#L277-L305) — single TCP probe and startup gate
- [trial.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/trial.py#L1356-L1365) — lockdown before agent launch
- [lockdown_smoke.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f07e07ac26ef2457f98cb7a7adfa7e96e9c031a0/experiments/post_training/tmax_reserve/lockdown_smoke.py#L98-L121) — delayed probe

# Proposed Fix

1. Reproduce at the pilot's 64-concurrent-sandbox setting. Record the update-return time, immediate and repeated TCP results, a request for recognizable PyPI content, an allow-listed `iris.oa.dev` control request, and sandbox IDs. Keep agents stopped during diagnostics; classify proxy denial, upstream content, and inconclusive requests separately.
2. If TCP succeeds while the proxy denies HTTPS, replace the TCP-only gate with a probe that recognizes the denial and fails closed on inconclusive results. Add a behavioral regression test.
3. If PyPI content is reachable after the update, measure how long it remains reachable, report sandbox IDs and timestamps to Daytona, and add a bounded verification wait that never starts the agent while the probe is reachable or inconclusive.
4. Validate on a comparable 64-concurrent cohort with enough updates to compare against the pilot's 9/1600 failures. Report the observed failure rate and any confirmed disallowed HTTPS responses.
